items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Claude Fable 5.2 (claude-fable-5-2), now the default Fable model — 1M context, $8/$40 per Mtok with $0.20/Mtok cache reads
  • Added --settings <file> to claude remote-control, which applies a settings file to every session it starts; if the file changes, no new session starts until you restart claude remote-control
  • Fixed MCP OAuth requests sending secrets such as refresh tokens to another host when a server redirected them
  • Fixed a case where a read-only Bash command ran outside the sandbox without a permission prompt
  • Fixed a case where Bash permission checks judged a file write from the wrong folder and didn't prompt
  • Fixed deny rules and protected-file prompts not applying to the file that a cp or mv into a directory writes
  • Fixed the "Draws from usage credits" note showing after a switch to Fable on Enterprise seats whose plan includes Fable
  • Fixed the fallback model sometimes declining a request or mentioning a stopped response when the first model was blocked before replying
  • Fixed claude mcp login printing a SEP-2352 issuer warning each time you sign in again to a server that Claude Code registered with
  • Fixed NotebookEdit deleting or overwriting a notebook's first cell when the call named no cell, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed Edit changing the first of several matches, replacing a whole file on an empty old_string, or editing a notebook as text, on network paths (UNC shares, WSL folders, /net mounts)
  • Fixed /config showing Manual as the default permission mode when new sessions start in auto mode; pressing Space on "Auto (default)" now saves Don't Ask, not Plan
  • Windows: Fixed FileChanged hooks stopping for paths set through watchPaths after the first shell command, when the session's working directory had a lowercase drive letter
  • Fixed --plugin-dir . and --plugin-dir ./builtin writing generated type files for Claude Code's built-in plugins into a builtin folder
  • Fixed context usage estimates overcounting tool definitions when exact token counts are unavailable
  • Fixed /compact showing twice in Remote Control on web and mobile
  • Fixed plugin auto-updates and /plugin marketplace updates downloading a plugin again for each worktree or folder of a repository
  • Fixed auto mode losing a background subagent's report that had started a turn when the conversation was compacted before Claude answered it
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents staying missing after their folder was removed and came back mid-session, such as with git stash, including after entering a worktree
  • Fixed claude -p sometimes telling Claude that background commands get 30 minutes when they are stopped after 10
  • Fixed pkill, pgrep and pidwait in cloud sessions matching the session's own parent processes
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome and computer use server processes staying alive after their parent exits behind a proxy that stalls connections
  • Fixed a large hook output pointing Claude to a file that held another hook's output from the same tool call
  • Fixed apps that embed Claude Code getting their own PreToolUse hook's ask reason instead of another hook's when both asked
  • Fixed a PreToolUse hook's ask being lost when another hook's defer finished first and could not be honored
  • Fixed a rare crash on permission prompts and background tasks
  • Fixed project skills, commands and agents disappearing from the menu in SDK and desktop sessions after Claude entered a worktree
  • Fixed /desktop on macOS saying Claude Desktop is not installed when it is in ~/Applications
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry repository attributes (vcs.*) missing from Claude Desktop sessions that start on a pre-started process
  • Fixed WebFetch passing "No response from model" to Claude as page content when the model reading the page returned no text; the call now fails with a clear error
  • Fixed screen reader mode delaying the prompt at startup when the system clock moved back while Claude Code was starting
  • Fixed a command's panel sometimes not coming back after a dialog closed, leaving no panel or prompt on screen until the next redraw
  • Fixed a project's MCP server being disconnected after the first message in a Claude Desktop Code tab session when the desktop app has an MCP server or extension of the same name
  • Fixed a turn ending with "API Error: EPROTO: The TLS handshake failed" when the connection broke partway through a reply; the partial reply is kept or the request is retried, as before 2.1.302
  • Fixed high memory use in long sessions that repeatedly read single lines from large files
  • Fixed fast mode losing replies, switching models or retrying for minutes when fast serving is rate-limited, overloaded or failing; it now tries standard speed on the same model first
  • Fixed one request carrying far more background agent reports than intended after Claude was stopped while several were waiting
  • Fixed messages from a Claude Desktop Code tab session to your other sessions staying paused after you typed while Claude was still working
  • Fixed claude agents ignoring --permission-mode, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --model, --effort or --agent typed before agents when a flag such as --verbose was also on the line
  • Fixed a case where Remote Control showed as off with "login expired" in the desktop app while its connection was still up, because the app was briefly unable to hand over a sign-in token
  • Fixed a Remote Control message sent with "Queue for later" reaching Claude in the middle of the running turn
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start reading as clean when git status failed; it now reads as unavailable
  • Fixed the git status given to Claude at session start showing the first listed file as staged when its changes were not staged
  • Fixed a hang or out-of-memory crash when a connector in a cloud session lists resources with very long names
  • Fixed Remote Control showing as connected after its connection closed for good while the session's history was still uploading
  • Fixed screen reader mode turning off when you return to a conversation from agent view
  • Fixed screen reader mode y/n questions taking as yes a stray "y" at the end of text typed as the question opened
  • Fixed cloud sessions telling Claude that a host is probably not allowed when it is allowed and the network proxy could not connect to it
  • Fixed an MCP server sometimes showing as connected with no tools after it was reconnected or the session's directory changed while its tools were still loading
  • Fixed Bash commands sometimes running in the wrong folder when Claude sent several at once and an earlier one changed folders
  • Fixed files Claude sends from cloud and Remote Control sessions failing at once when an upload gets an HTTP 507 from a proxy; the upload now gets a second try
  • Fixed new messages not being saved, and claude -p, SDK and VS Code sessions hanging, when memory ran out while the transcript was being read
  • Fixed sign-in, token refresh and logout waiting indefinitely when something on the network accepts the connection but never answers the TLS handshake
  • Fixed a sent file showing under a different name in the Claude apps when its name hid text-direction or control characters; Claude now refuses to send such a file
  • Fixed sub-agent progress summaries running a request to its end after the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed Bash reads such as grep -r foo "$PWD/src" asking for permission when the same command with the path typed out runs without asking
  • Fixed Claude apps gateway refusing to start when a desktop setting holds a field newer than the gateway, such as a managed MCP server's oauth.omitResource; it now warns and serves it
  • Fixed Bash commands coming back empty for zsh users whose .zshrc sets KSH_OPTION_PRINT
  • macOS: Fixed "Unable to read managed policy settings" at startup when a valid MDM profile was slow to read: the read is retried once, and a timeout is now reported as a timeout
  • Fixed agent view erasing another agent view's saved input text when it restarted for an update with nothing typed
  • Fixed remote sessions giving no reply after a restart when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocked a replayed permission answer; these hooks no longer run on that replay
  • Fixed claude remote-control accepting a y typed without Enter at its first-run question when the terminal's input ended
  • Fixed Claude Desktop not showing spend limit warnings behind a Claude apps gateway whose policy has no code: rules
  • Fixed fullscreen sessions with some plugins ending with an error when a tool result that had got shorter scrolled off the top of the screen
  • Fixed prompt suggestions making extra API requests when the model replied with a tool call
  • Fixed PreToolUse mcp_tool hooks on stdio and HTTP MCP servers being skipped when their answer was over 16 MiB; the tool call is now refused
  • Fixed skill and command names holding a Bamum letter that some fonts draw as blank: they are now refused
  • Fixed claude -p on Linux exiting 0 in silence when a full NFS export or a used-up NFS quota lost transcript lines: it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1
  • Fixed background agents being reported as stopped by the user, and refused a resume, when a service interrupted a cloud session and nobody pressed Stop
  • Fixed NotebookEdit reporting success to hooks and telemetry when the edit failed, for example when the notebook changed while the permission prompt was open
  • Fixed a blank screen or no answer at startup, and empty claude mcp list output, when a stored MCP sign-in record was null
  • Fixed the Artifact tool telling Claude to add filters when an artifact's database collection is too large to sort; it now says to read the collection page by page and sort the results
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session dropping a message with a large image when the restart came before Claude's first reply to it
  • Fixed a restarted cloud session leaving a subagent's message to the main conversation unanswered
  • Fixed Claude not being told when you stop or pause a running workflow, so it no longer says the workflow is still running
  • Improved the /model picker: "More models" is now an unnumbered row below every other, and older models open under it without renumbering the rest
  • Gateway: Improved spend limits on a busy replica, which now skips fewer checks and records spend sooner
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's sign-in limit messages in Claude Code and on the /device page: they no longer name gateway settings, which the gateway's own log still names
  • Improved claude install and the install scripts: they finish 2 to 4 seconds sooner
  • Improved how soon a Remote Control session whose process crashed can pick up a new message
  • Windows: Improved startup and first-command time by finding programs on PATH without starting a helper process
  • Improved auto mode in headless sessions, the desktop app and VS Code: reports from background subagents that wait together are answered in one model call, as in the terminal
  • Improved the agent view's row for a claude --bg --worktree session that couldn't set up its worktree: it now shows the error from its beginning, not an internal tag or its last 200 characters
  • Improved the messages shown when an artifact is in another organization: /login is offered only if it's one of yours, and Claude now says where a copy may be after an account move
  • Improved sessions with more images than fit in one request: Claude is told whether it has already seen a dropped image, and repeat reads of an unchanged image are limited
  • Improved claude remote-control's messages for an unanswered first-run question: each now says what to do next
  • Improved start-up time by loading trusted TLS certificates faster
  • Improved Claude apps gateway error messages to show the gateway's address without any user name or password
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: the reset now shows in your local time, such as "resets 4pm (America/Los_Angeles)"
  • Windows: Improved startup time with a standard Git for Windows install by no longer checking which git.exe to run on every launch
  • Updated the session-feedback message and the allowedProviders setting description to name Ultra alongside Pro and Max, and the forceLoginMethod description to cover every paid Claude plan
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to suggest a list of meters, one row per item, for several ratios that each have their own limit
  • Updated the "Upgrade to Max" options to say "Upgrade to Max or Ultra"
  • Changed mods Claude writes to turn on without asking in auto and bypass modes, even with managed allowUnsandboxedCommands: false or allowManagedDomainsOnly, and not to load in dontAsk mode
  • Changed mods' own tool calls ($.tool.call, $.mcp.call) to raise no permission prompt, even under your own ask rules or in dontAsk and -p runs; deny rules and organization policy still apply
  • Changed saved Fable 5.1 model picks to move to fable: on Pro and Max plans at once, on Team and Enterprise plans once your organization allows it; use /model claude-fable-5-1 to switch back
  • Changed the fast mode labels in /fast, /config and /model to name your current model when it supports fast mode, and removed "(Opus only)" from the VS Code row
  • Changed nested skill loading: .claude/skills folders inside ~/.claude/plugins no longer load when Claude works on files there
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed an on-demand runner that the server refuses because it is not needed (session ended or paused, work order superseded) to exit 0 instead of 1
  • Windows: Changed how Claude Code finds programs it starts itself, such as git, to skip relative and UNC PATH entries and links onto a network share, and to pick up PATH changes from settings
  • Changed OpenTelemetry hook events in non-interactive sessions to leave two built-in hooks out of num_hooks and num_success after Bash and PowerShell calls
  • Changed the number of messages a Claude Desktop Code tab session can send to your other sessions before it waits for you to type again from 10 to 20
  • Changed AskUserQuestion in claude -p and SDK sessions to deny a host's permission answer that sets the undocumented afkTimeoutMs input field
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces: a declared name can't be added from another source, an entry from elsewhere is hidden, and plugins the declared marketplace lists are reinstalled from it
  • Changed Claude in Chrome tools that an app running Claude Code provides, such as the Claude desktop app's Code tab, to follow your organization's Claude in Chrome policy
  • Changed policy_mode: layered in the Claude apps gateway: managed MCP servers now add up over every matching policy, match: {} included, so a gateway already on it serves more after the upgrade
  • Gateway: Changed Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry upstreams to ignore the ANTHROPIC_*_BASE_URL variables in the gateway's environment. Set base_url on the upstream to use another endpoint
  • Changed headless sessions to reload mods in .claude/skills when their files change; set CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIR_WATCH=0 to turn this off
  • Changed the Cyber Verification Program sentence on a cyber safeguard block to use the same words as claude.ai
  • Changed Cowork cloud sessions: a PostToolUse hook can no longer replace the answer to AskUserQuestion or the plan in ExitPlanMode's result; Claude reads the originals
  • Changed cp and mv spelled by a path, such as /bin/cp, to get the same path checks as cp and mv
  • Changed background command notifications and TaskStop results to show Claude only the start and end of a command over 1,000 characters, which saves context
  • Changed artifact design guidance to treat Inter and Space Grotesk as good default typefaces
  • Changed the account email check to refuse only a shell command that holds your email and names a User-Agent, without asking, so other commands and scheduled runs no longer stop at its prompt
  • Changed Remote Control sessions to keep the folder they were started in: a connected client can no longer move a session to another folder
  • Changed managed extraKnownMarketplaces take-overs from an undeclared source: saved data is set aside for cleanupPeriodDays, and options and secrets until claude plugin restore-set-aside
  • [VSCode] Added a warning above the prompt box when both an auth token and an API key are set, matching the terminal's startup warning
  • [VSCode] Fixed a plugin's permission request showing a name with hidden characters: it now reads "a plugin"

items.title: What Is Eval-Driven Development? How to Improve AI Agents
items.summary:
• Eval-driven development (EDD) involves building an agent while measuring performance against a consistent set of metrics and hill climbing toward an eval.
  • The first step of EDD is to create a short spec of what good looks like for your desired behavior. Include what the agent shouldn't do and what has to keep working.
  • As you iterate, judge a change you make to the agent by comparing experiments. A change that fixes one case may break another.
  • Keep evals running in CI and in production, and turn the failures you find into new dataset examples.

Development on most agents starts the same way. You write a prompt, try a few questions by hand, adjust, and try again. This works well in the beginning, when agent errors are obvious and improvements are easy to see. But over time it becomes increasingly difficult to know whether your most recent change made an agent better or worse.

Eval-driven development (EDD) solves this by giving you a consistent set of metrics to measure your agent’s performance against and guide your decision making. Here at LangChain we've used EDD when building our most advanced agents (check out our blog on IssueBench), and have boiled it down to a three step process:

  1. Define what good looks like for your agent.
  2. Write the eval before you build.
  3. Make your change and compare.

In this blog, we'll walk through this process step by step so that your team can apply it to your own agent development process.

What is eval-driven development?

The name and concept of eval-driven development borrows from test-driven development (TDD), where you write a failing test before writing the code that passes it. Agents differ from traditional code as they're non-deterministic:

  • Outputs vary. The same question can receive a different answer on each run.
  • More than one answer can be right. Two natural language results can both be considered correct despite using different phrasing.
  • The agent chooses its own steps. It might call a tool it didn't need, or skip one it should have used, and still reach the correct answer.

As a result, agents need a different kind of test. An eval handles this by scoring runs of your agent across a set of examples. Evals are more flexible than traditional testing. You can score any aspect of the agent's run and you can use other LLMs to score it (LLM-as-a-judge).

With EDD, similar to TDD, these evals become your definition of success and you build your agent towards them.

Step 1: Define what good looks like for your agent

The first step in EDD is defining what your agent should do. Then, list the behaviors it needs to handle to get there. These could be tasks such as answering questions from a knowledge base, taking an action on a user's behalf, or knowing when to ask a follow-up question. Write down the requirements for each behavior. Together, these make up a product requirements document (PRD) for your agent.

EDD works on one behavior at a time. This gives you a narrow target to hill climb toward, without one change muddying the effect of another. The behavior you pick usually comes from a feature you're about to build or a failure you found in your agent's past runs. Before writing code, it’s helpful to define a short spec that covers:

  • When the behavior should happen
  • What the agent should do
  • What the agent shouldn't do
  • Which behaviors from your PRD must keep working

The spec should be definitive enough to score as a pass or fail.

Say we have an internal docs agent that employees query for company information. It has two tools: search_docs for internal documentation and web_search for everything else. We plan to add a create_ticket tool so it can file IT tickets. Our spec looks like this:

  • When: A user reports something broken, like "My laptop won't connect to the VPN."
  • Do: Call create_ticket.
  • Don't: File a ticket for how-to questions, like “How do I connect to the VPN?”
  • Keep intact: search_docs and web_search still handle the questions they handle today

We’ll evaluate on these guidelines, even though the agent doesn’t have the capability yet.

Step 2: Write the eval before you build

Build a dataset. A dataset is a collection of test cases (called “examples”) that have inputs and, optionally, reference “golden” outputs. One of the best sources for inputs is real agent runs. Users can phrase things in ways you wouldn't predict, and their requests include edge cases you may not think to write yourself. If your examples look like real traffic, a good score on your eval is more likely to mean good behavior in production. In LangSmith, you can directly add real agent runs to a dataset. If you don’t have any runs yet, a common alternative is to build your examples from scratch.

For our docs agent, a handful of examples is enough to start. In our dataset, we’ll include ticket requests, plus questions that should still go to search_docs and web_search so existing behavior is accounted for.

You can also extend your dataset to cover cases it doesn't have yet. Say we don't have many examples of frustrated users. We could give our existing examples to an LLM, ask it to rewrite them as angrier messages, and check that the agent still calls the right tool.

Write an evaluator. Once you have your dataset, you can take your definition of "good" from your PRD and turn that into a test or eval that scores your agent’s performance on your examples. When writing an evaluator, choose which type of scoring method works best for your test. Use a code eval when the check is deterministic, and an LLM-as-a-judge when it isn't. Do you want to look at the agent's final answer, an action it’s taken to get there, or something else entirely? For our docs agent, we want to look at the tools it calls to verify it’s using the right ones in each case. Tool choice is easy to check in code, so we can use a code eval to check whether each example called the tool listed in its reference output.

Our docs agent is a simple chatbot with a few specific functions. As your agent becomes increasingly complex, your eval suite will likely need to look a little different. If your agent makes changes in an environment, like a coding agent in a sandbox, checking a couple of tool calls and the final response doesn't tell you enough. You need to check the state the agent leaves behind in the system, and each run needs a clean environment so one run doesn't affect the next. Harbor is an open source framework for running agents on tasks like these, and it's the harness behind industry benchmarks like Terminal-Bench. Each task runs in its own sandbox and comes with a test script that grades the end state.

Optimizing for a benchmark like Terminal-Bench follows the same loop as EDD. You write the tasks and tests first, run a baseline, and compare experiments as you make changes to the agent. When we built LangSmith Engine, we made our own benchmark from both real and synthetic agent runs and ran it as a Harbor eval. We also use Harbor to benchmark Deep Agents. It tells us whether we can cut parts of the harness, like the todo-list middleware or parts of the system prompt, without making the agent worse.

Run a baseline. However you choose to build your dataset or evaluator, you can run your agent on every example and log the results as an experiment in LangSmith. An experiment is a single run of your agent over the dataset, where each example's input, output, and evaluator scores are saved together in one record. Having a centralized system allows you to compare results from different agent versions to one another. Before making any changes to your agent, it’s important to run a baseline experiment as a comparison metric.

With our docs agent, the ticket examples in the dataset get a failing score, since the tool doesn't exist yet. The other examples record what already works, so you can tell later if adding a new tool breaks something else.

Step 3: Make your change and compare

Now, we build the create_ticket tool and run the same eval.

Remember that EDD involves “hill-climbing” toward an eval. Hill-climbing means repeating the process of improving the agent (evaluating, comparing, and adjusting) so you can establish a defined loop with objective evidence of improvement. Each subsequent change to the agent gets its own experiment, and each experiment is compared to the last one to verify progress. In LangSmith, you can open the comparison view by selecting both experiments. It shows the scores side by side for each example, so you can see which ones improved and which ones regressed.

When comparing experiments, it’s important to be aware of not just changes in the average score, but also any regressions or overwriting of working behavior. With our docs agent, the ticket examples now pass. But "How do I connect to the VPN?" now files a ticket instead of searching the docs. The average score went up, but one case broke.

Reviewing a trace is the best way to understand why an eval failed. A trace is a record of one run of your agent, including every model call and tool call. Tracing is possible in LangSmith with any agent built using your choice of framework. For more info check out our tracing quickstart.

When we open the failing trace for the latest experiment, we see that the tool description says to use create_ticket for "VPN and laptop issues," so any question that mentions the VPN matches. This overwrites the baseline good behavior.

The solution is to narrow the tool description to requests that need IT to act. After implementing this change, we run the eval again. Now, every example passes.

A perfect score on a small dataset is a good sign, but 100% isn't always the right target. We tuned the tool description while looking at these exact examples. If you keep adjusting the agent until every example passes, it can start overfitting to your dataset instead of the behavior you care about. It passes your eval and still misses requests phrased in ways your examples don't cover. To check for this, keep a held-out set of examples you don't look at while iterating. If your score goes up on the examples you tune against but stays flat on the held-out set, you're likely overfitting.

Multi-step agents can fail at any step, so LangSmith lets you evaluate more than the final answer. You can score a single step, the full sequence of tool calls, or a multi-turn conversation grouped into a thread.

Keep EDD running as you ship

Automating your evals

As you begin to deploy changes faster, it’s easy to skip running evals or lose track of older examples. By adding automated evaluation to your workflow, you can prevent untested changes from reaching users and catch regressions pre-production.

The best strategy for creating your eval suite depends on your individual set up. Fast code checks can block a bad merge, while slower evals with LLM judges can run nightly or before a release. Use dataset splits to run only the examples for the behavior you're working on while iterating, then the full set before you ship.

LangSmith integrates with pytest and Vitest, so your evals can sit next to your code and run on every pull request. Each run is logged as an experiment, so you can view results in the same place as everything else.

Evaluating in production

Prior to deploying your agent, your dataset likely only covers the cases you thought to test in development. In production you can flag the rest, using the following evaluation methods:

  • Online evaluators score live traces as they come in. You can attach code checks and LLM judges to a tracing project and sample a share of traffic to manage cost.
  • Annotation queues let your team review flagged runs by hand. They're also how you check that an LLM judge agrees with people before you rely on it.
  • Dashboards can track eval scores, feedback, cost, and latency over time, so you can see whether a release made things better or worse.
  • Insights groups production traces into clusters so you can spot new patterns across thousands of runs.
  • LangSmith Engine takes it a step further and turns clusters of issues into dataset examples with assertions for you to review.

We've also published the evals we use for Deep Agents in its repo, so you can see a real, production eval suite.

Common mistakes

  • Defining success too loosely. Do the heavy lifting up front to clearly define success so that evals can easily score for a pass or fail. “The response is helpful” is not a well-defined metric.
  • Writing the eval after the fix. Once you've seen new output, it's easy to write an eval that passes by design. Write it first and confirm it fails on the current broken version.
  • Only checking the average score. Improvements in the average score can hide examples that regressed or changes that overwrote good behavior. Review each example before you decide to keep a change.
  • Adding evals you don't need. Each eval pushes the agent in some direction. Tie each eval to a specific change, like a failure you're fixing or a feature you're about to build.
  • Trusting an unchecked judge. Compare your LLM judge against human scores first. Ask it narrow questions and use pass or fail instead of an ambiguous 1 to 10 scale.

For more info about building agent evals, check out this webinar on Agent Evals 101 and our free LangChain Academy course on LangSmith!

Further reading:

  • The most common questions about agent evals, answered
  • How we build evals for Deep Agents
  • Towards automating eval engineering
  • LangSmith evaluation quickstart

items.summary:
For more information about Stanford’s graduate programs, visit:

What’s actually happening when you chat with an AI? This opening lecture demystifies large language models from the ground up — tokens, neural networks, weights and layers, and the two-stage journey from training to inference that turns raw text into a working chatbot. Along the way we introduce the concepts (context windows, transformers, attention) that explain both what makes modern AI so capable and why it still confidently gets things wrong, including hallucination, sycophancy, and the pull to anthropomorphize a fundamentally statistical tool. No coding or technical background required — by the end, you’ll have a working mental model for what AI can and can’t do, which every later lecture builds on.

Speaker: Cynthia Bailey

Cynthia Bailey is a Senior Lecturer in the Computer Science Department at Stanford University. In 2023-2024, she served as an AI Policy Fellow in the United States Senate through the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS). Her scholarship focuses on computer science education, AI/machine learning, and the social impacts of technology. This work includes creating groundbreaking courses such as Equity and Governance for Artificial Intelligence and Race and Gender in Silicon Valley. Her teaching and research awards include the Lloyd W. Dinkelspiel Award for exceptional contributions to undergraduate education at Stanford, the Lasting Impact Award from the International Computing Education Research conference, a "Top 10 Papers of All Time" award at the 50th anniversary of the ACM SIGCSE Technical Symposium, and the Stanford Society of Women Engineers' Professor of the Year. She has consulted for Apple, NASA, law firms, and machine learning startups. She holds a Ph.D. in Computer Science from UC San Diego.

items.title: Extending LLDB to Debug Applications That Span CPUs and GPUs
items.summary:
We built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server for debugging applications that span CPUs and GPUs. It separates shared debugger infrastructure from hardware-specific device control. The design represents the CPU and GPU as separate debugger processes while presenting them in one debugging session. Modern AI applications rarely execute in one place. A workload can [...]

Read More...

The post Extending LLDB to Debug Applications That Span CPUs and GPUs appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
items.content:
• We built a vendor-neutral accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server for debugging applications that span CPUs and GPUs. It separates shared debugger infrastructure from hardware-specific device control.
  • The design represents the CPU and GPU as separate debugger processes while presenting them in one debugging session.

Modern AI applications rarely execute in one place. A workload can begin in a high-level framework and move back and forth between native CPU code and kernels running on a GPU. When a bug crosses those boundaries, developers need to understand the host application and the device together.

That is harder than attaching a conventional debugger to another process. The CPU and GPU may use different instruction sets, registers, memory spaces, and execution models. The GPU is also controlled through a runtime and driver inside the host process, so debugging the device often requires careful coordination with the CPU.

Historically, GPU vendors built device-specific debuggers, including AMD’s ROCgdb and NVIDIA’s CUDA-GDB. These tools provide deep support for their respective platforms, but common debugger capabilities must often be implemented and maintained separately.

At Meta, we have been developing a different approach for LLDB: a common accelerator plugin architecture in lldb-server. In this post, “GPU” refers to the concrete devices and examples, while “accelerator” refers to LLDB’s broader, vendor-neutral plugin abstraction. The architecture has evolved through contributions from engineers at Meta and across the accelerator ecosystem. It keeps the shared debugger independent of any one GPU while giving hardware vendors a focused place to implement device-specific behavior.

Why GPU Debugging Challenges Traditional Debugger Models

A traditional debugger generally assumes that one process has one architecture and a consistent view of threads, registers, and memory. GPU programs challenge each of those assumptions.

A host process might run on x86-64 while its kernels use a completely different instruction set. A CPU thread has a familiar register context, while a GPU may execute groups of lanes in lockstep. Host and device pointers can refer to different address spaces. A GPU can expose thousands of execution lanes, which do not map cleanly onto the thread model that most command-line and graphical debuggers present.

Combining all of this state into one artificial process model makes the debugger more complicated. Every operation must first determine whether it applies to the CPU or the GPU. Register handling, memory reads, breakpoints, stepping, and stop events all become conditional on the selected hardware. A single process model also forces the CPU and GPU into one unified memory map, even though their address spaces can be independent: The same address, such as 0x1000, can refer to different locations in the CPU and GPU processes.

Instead of hiding those differences, the LLDB accelerator architecture gives them a clear boundary.

Plugin Support in lldb-server for GPU Debugging

LLDB uses a companion process called lldb-server to launch or attach to a program and perform low-level debugging operations. The LLDB client communicates with the server through the GDB remote protocol, a command protocol for operations such as reading memory, inspecting registers, controlling execution, and setting breakpoints.

Because lldb-server already controls the native process, it is also the right place to coordinate with an accelerator runtime. The new plugin interface lets a hardware-specific backend work alongside the normal CPU debugger. The backend translates a vendor’s device debugging API into concepts LLDB already understands, such as processes, threads, registers, memory, modules, and stop reasons.

This separation keeps the LLDB client vendor-neutral. Common improvements to the command line, remote protocol, symbol handling, and IDE integration can benefit every accelerator. At the same time, each vendor remains responsible for the details that are unique to its hardware and driver stack.

GPU debugging support is activated only when the debugged application uses a supported GPU runtime. For CPU-only applications, LLDB and lldb-server continue through the existing native debugging path without incurring runtime computational overhead.

Two Targets, One Debugging Experience

The architecture represents the CPU and accelerator as separate LLDB targets.
Each target has its own architecture and is associated with a debugger process that maintains its threads, registers, address space, and execution state. The CPU continues to use LLDB’s established native debugging path. When the accelerator becomes available, the plugin provides a second connection that LLDB uses to create the device target.

To the debugger, the two targets remain technically independent. To the developer, they can appear in one LLDB or IDE session. This avoids forcing incompatible CPU and GPU concepts into a single process while still supporting a unified workflow.

Coordinating the Host and Device

A typical debugging session follows a small set of steps:

  1. LLDB connects to lldb-server and discovers which accelerator plugins are available.
  2. A plugin can ask LLDB to set internal breakpoints in the host process. These breakpoints identify important runtime events, such as the point at which a GPU debugging session can begin.
  3. When the host reaches one of those points, lldb-server notifies the plugin. The plugin initializes the vendor debugging API and prepares an accelerator debugging endpoint.
  4. LLDB creates a second target for the accelerator and connects to it. Device threads, registers, memory, modules, and breakpoints can then use LLDB’s existing abstractions.

Structured actions coordinate the two sides. A plugin can request CPU breakpoints, provide connection information, report device modules, and synchronize host and device execution. The common protocol describes what the debugger needs to do without exposing vendor-specific API details to the LLDB client.

We also built a mock accelerator plugin that exercises this flow without specialized hardware. It lets the LLVM test suite verify discovery, breakpoint coordination, connection creation, and basic device state. This has been important for developing shared infrastructure that can be reviewed and tested independently of any particular GPU.

A Typical GPU Workflow

The vector dot-product HIP sample produced this abridged session:

(lldb) target list
Current targets:
  target #0: gpu_demo (x86_64, stopped)
* target #1: amd_memory_kernel[...] (amdgcn, stopped)

(lldb) b compute_element
Breakpoint 1: no locations (pending).
(lldb) c
(lldb) target select 0
(lldb) c
Launching kernel: 2 blocks x 32 threads
1 location added to breakpoint 1
Target 1 stopped.

(lldb) target select 1
(lldb) bt
* frame #0: compute_element(..., idx=32) at gpu_demo.hip:26
  frame #1: vector_dot_kernel(..., n=64) at gpu_demo.hip:35
The pending breakpoint resolves when the GPU module loads, and the backtrace
comes from the GPU target.

A Common Plugin Framework Across Hardware Vendors

The plugin boundary is intentionally based on debugger operations rather than concepts from a specific GPU platform. That makes it useful across devices with very different instruction sets, runtime APIs, and execution models.

The framework supports postmortem GPU debugging as well as live sessions. GPU core-dump plugins use a common base class for their LLDB integration, while vendor implementations provide the device-specific thread, register, memory, and module state.

GPU debugging efforts at Meta are already leveraging the architecture. Because we operate a heterogeneous fleet of GPUs with different hardware and software stacks, the fact that these efforts use the same model is an important validation of the design: the common LLDB layer can remain stable while each backend represents its own device accurately.

At the time of writing, we have upstreamed most of the common framework to LLVM. This includes the lldb-server plugin interface; GDB-remote packets for plugin discovery, initialization, runtime-event coordination, and GPU connection creation; support for associating CPU and GPU debugger processes while preserving their independent architecture; support for multiple address spaces, and hardware-independent mock tests. We expect to upstream the remaining pieces soon.

Looking Ahead

Next, we plan to finish upstreaming the remaining common infrastructure and expand the vendor integrations built on it. Our goal is that integrating new hardware with LLDB should require only a vendor-specific plugin, not a separate debugger to build and maintain. 

Acknowledgements 

We are grateful to Meta’s Developer Infrastructure leadership team, especially Shane Nay, Todd Fiala, and Ale Contenti, whose direct support made this work possible.

We also thank our Debugging & Tooling teammates Jacob Lalonde, David Young, Alexandre Perez, Zhiyuan Li, Piyush Jaiswal, and Philip DePetro for their collaboration and support.

Finally, we thank the open source community, especially Jonas Devlieghere, Jim Ingham, David Spickett, and Jason Molenda, for reviewing the RFCs and upstream pull requests.

Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
items.summary: Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components.  The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in […]
items.content:
Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components. 

The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) in Austin, Texas, alongside the rise of agentic robotics — a new paradigm that integrates frontier agents to create interpretable code for physical robotics systems.

At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing new open robotics technologies, including world action models, simulation tools, benchmarks and agentic workflows. 

Two NVIDIA papers are among six finalists out of thousands of submissions for the Best Paper Awards at CoRL: 

  • GRAIL (Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models), which presents a digital generation pipeline for 3D assets and simulator-ready scenes for robot learning.
  • RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies, which introduces a robot model and training recipe that scales visuomotor context three orders of magnitude beyond state-of-the-art policies without growing inference latency.

These advancements help researchers train robots on complex tasks, evaluate their performance across changing conditions and use failures to guide further learning — building the precision, adaptability and autonomy needed to move from lab demonstrations to industrial deployment. 

NVIDIA is working with partners like Ambi Robotics, Bosch Research, Dexmate, Dyna Robotics, FieldAI, Flexion, Noitom Robotics, Siemens, Skild AI, RLWRLD, UC Berkeley, Walden Robotics and the University of Washington to bring these advancements to the broader robotics community.  

World Action Models Enable Next Level of Robot Autonomy

The next level of robot autonomy requires robots to perceive their surroundings, anticipate how their actions will change the environment and execute complex, multistep tasks with a high degree of precision. World action models enable exactly that.

At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing GR00T 2, an open frontier world action model built on NVIDIA Cosmos. Trained on diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of NVIDIA open source human egocentric data, the model enables robots to learn dexterous manipulation skills. Key features include:

  • Out-of-the-box performance: Completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations.
  • Skill transfer: Learns from human demonstrations and transfers skills between different robot bodies without robot demonstrations
  • Generalization with little data: Achieved 71% average success across 50 tasks with just one demonstration per task, increasing to 95% with five.
  • Agent control: AI agents can use GR00T 2’s application programming interface and supporting tools to run skills in sequence and recover from errors.

 

GR00T 2 currently ranks among the top three models across all vision language action and world action model categories for the RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo and MolmoSpaces benchmarks, with multiple leaderboard wins.  

Nexuni is testing it for robotic laundry handling, Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing and Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases.

MicroAGI is using GR00T 2, post-trained through reinforcement learning, to perform Ethernet cable swapping with a YAM robotic arm. Its agentic robotics approach automates the creation and calibration of simulation environments using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton, where the policy is trained.

Training capable robots requires diverse data. Open NVIDIA workflows and models equip researchers with better tools for data collection and annotation:

  • For researchers building robot-training datasets, NVIDIA’s new open Video to Data workflow turns human video into simulated robot demonstrations, with a challenge inviting researchers to advance it.
  • The NVIDIA EgoHand open model — being demoed at CoRL and with over 40,000 Hugging Face downloads in the two weeks since launch — reconstructs 3D hand motion, trained with data from Noitom Robotics.

 

Where the Training and Scaling Happens — in Simulation

A pretrained model gives robots a core set of skills. Simulation lets researchers train, refine and evaluate skills at scale before deploying them on physical robots. 

NVIDIA Isaac Lab, an open source robot-learning framework, provides the foundation for that work. Its latest release, Isaac Lab 3.0, allows researchers to use agents to quickly set up training environments with simulation-ready assets, switch between NVIDIA PhysX and Newton physics solvers, choose renderers for perception-based training and apply a new reinforcement post-training library to foundation models like GR00T.

Accurate physics is critical to transferring learned skills from simulation to the real robot. Tighter integration with Newton, an open source physics engine, now allows Isaac Lab to model deformable objects such as cables and cloth, along with complex articulated systems such as robotic hands with many interacting joints. 

Integration with Newton simulates how a strawberry deforms under a robot’s grip.

Together, Isaac Lab and Newton combine accurate physics with scale to enable researchers to train thousands of simulated robots in parallel. In a vision-based dexterous manipulation benchmark, Isaac Lab 3.0 with Newton achieved up to 2.5x the training throughput of Isaac Lab 2.3 with PhysX.

Isaac Lab supports robot simulation with Newton and NVIDIA PhysX.

Developers are extending Newton’s capabilities. At CoRL, Skild AI announced Scalable Throughput-optimized Engine for Embodied Learning, or STEEL, a new rigid-body physics solver built on Newton to accelerate robot training with Isaac Lab.

Skild AI’s STEEL Solver.

Flexion showcased how Isaac Lab and Newton help train Reflect, its robot-intelligence model combining reasoning and whole-body manipulation. 

Flexion uses Newton for RL with Isaac Lab.

FieldAI is using Newton — as well as Isaac Lab and Isaac Sim, built on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries — to train and validate robot policies for deployment in unstructured real-world environments. Dyna Robotics will demonstrate how parallel simulation in Isaac Lab helps train whole-body controllers for its semi-humanoid Taku robot for work in warehouses, hotels and food services.

Walden Robotics is using Isaac Sim’s photorealistic rendering to train and evaluate its general-purpose robot in virtual environments for manufacturing and logistics, while Dexmate is exploring how coding agents can rehearse and refine manipulation strategies in Isaac Sim before executing them on its Vega robot. 

AlphaNIST, built in Isaac Lab, demonstrates how efficient practice can translate into precision. A single policy learns all 20 tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board, manipulating  millimeter-scale parts using only a yes-or-no success signal. It achieves more than 98% training success, compared with 81% for separate per-task policies, using roughly 39x less GPU time.

AlphaNIST uses Isaac Lab to train a single robot policy across 20 precision tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board. 

Behind those results is Success-Guided Sampling, or SGS, from the University of Washington and NVIDIA. The method focuses practice on tasks a policy succeeds at about half the time, directing training toward skills it’s still learning. With SGS, robot training can scale beyond a million parallel environments. 

The University of Texas at Austin’s School of Computing and Texas Robotics uses Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab to train robotic skills in simulation, letting students start developing before physical hardware is available.

New Industrial Benchmarks for Robot Evaluation

Learning a skill is one challenge. Performing it reliably across changing conditions is another. 

NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena, an open source framework for scaled policy evaluation, enables developers to compose diverse and repeatable evaluations, then run policies across thousands of variations in parallel. Analyses expose which conditions cause failures, so researchers know what to fix in their next training run. The developer preview of its latest version, 0.4, is arriving at CoRL. 

DexBench and VABAR, two new open benchmarks, are among the first designed to measure robot dexterity and adaptability across industrial tasks using Isaac Lab-Arena and Newton.

DexBench, developed by RLWRLD in collaboration with NVIDIA, takes dexterity evaluation off the tabletop and into real-world workflows. Built using NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena, it features 15 tasks across four scenes spanning retail, logistics, manufacturing and hospitality, testing generalization across object, spatial and physics variations. 

Genesis AI, mimic robotics and other industry partners are evaluating DexBench through early access.

Teams can run DexBench on Manifold, Bifrost’s evaluation platform for scaling robotics simulations, with no setup required, built-in failure analysis and free credits for initial evaluations. 

VABAR — the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics — from UC Berkeley and NVIDIA, evaluates robots across six industrial tasks. Each carries standardized variations, difficulty tiers and success metrics. 

A simulated tool-sorting task demonstrates how VABAR evaluates robot manipulation skills for industrial workflows.

Agents Turn Skills Into Robot Programs

Successful task completion requires robots to coordinate multiple skills and adapt when something goes wrong. Building reliable programs for these multistep tasks remains a challenge.

Agentic robotics helps solve that challenge.

UC Berkeley’s new Graph-as-Policy (GaP) framework uses agents to connect individual skills into robot programs. Agents test these programs using NVIDIA Isaac open simulation technologies and refine them based on failures. This helps researchers scale development with less data while keeping the programs interpretable for engineers to review and verify before deployment.

GaP uses agents and simulation to turn individual robot skills into coordinated actions, such as wiping a bar.

“To me, agentic robotics is the most exciting technological development since the internet in 1995,” said Ken Goldberg, professor of robotics at UC Berkeley and a lead on the VABAR and GaP projects.

Ambi Robotics, Bosch Research and Siemens are all exploring GaP for its agentic robotics workflows across diverse industrial scenarios.

Learn more by joining NVIDIA at CoRL.

items.content:
Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT and NVIDIA hosted the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum at COEX.

Ryu Je-myung, vice minister of science and ICT, joined NVIDIA leaders to meet with over 20 Korean startups across foundation models, physical AI, AI infrastructure and AI semiconductors.

NVIDIA also announced an investment in Korean startup Point2, with additional investments planned in Motif Technologies, RLWRLD and Upstage. 

Point2 Technology, an AI interconnect company, builds scalable, radio frequency-based interconnects that move data between chips and racks in AI factories, offering an innovative alternative to conventional copper and optical interconnect solutions for AI cluster scale-up, delivering the reach, performance and efficiency needed for next-generation AI infrastructure.

Motif Technologies, a Seoul-based AI lab, develops foundation models for building AI agents that carry out complex tasks, including Motif-3, a large language model released with open weights.

RLWRLD, a physical AI startup based in San Francisco, Seoul and Tokyo, develops robotics foundation models that enable humanoid and industrial robots to perform complex real-world tasks that require five-finger dexterity, such as precisely inserting components, threading nuts onto bolts and kitting parts from moving conveyors. 

Upstage, a Korean enterprise AI company, develops Solar language models and document AI tools that help businesses extract information from complex documents, streamline workflows and build AI applications for everyday operations.

The companies represent work across the full AI stack, from infrastructure to models to robotics applications.

The planned investments build on NVIDIA’s work with Korea’s startup and venture community, including more than 1,000 Korea-based members of NVIDIA Inception, a program that helps startups grow with access to preferred pricing, technical expertise and opportunities for investor introductions.

Ari Azarafrooz, founder of Intrinsec AI, shows how the KV cache your inference engine already writes can double as a security signal for AI agents. Instead of only guarding inputs and outputs with judge models or a classifier for every failure, he learns a baseline from normal traffic and flags KV pages that look unusual, catching problems like a hidden spoken instruction in a voicemail where there is no text to filter. He covers where this plugs into stacks like vLLM, SGLang, LMCache, llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo, and the two hard parts in production: models that keep changing and KV data too big to move in real time.

items.title: Will AI Agents Pretend to Be Human to Get Past a Check? - Maty Bohacek, Stanford
items.summary:
Maty Bohacek of Stanford looks at a security check we still rely on: getting on a phone or video call to prove you're human before opening an account, approving a wire or recovering access. With AI avatars that can now join Zoom calls, he tested what agents do when a human check is the only thing between them and their goal. When a voice or video cloning tool was available, many agents used it to impersonate a person, even when told not to, and safety alignment only cut the rate from 65% to 44%. He closes with what needs to happen next across alignment, control, and deepfake detection and provenance.

items.summary:
Mislav Ivanda of Daytona has integrated sandboxes into most of the major agent frameworks, and noticed that frameworks that disagree on almost everything all ended up in the same place. He compares three ways to run agent-generated code: allow lists and approval prompts, embedded runtimes, and a separate sandboxed computer. He explains why only the last one keeps a compromised step from compromising your app, and shows frameworks like CrewAI, AG2 and the OpenAI Agents SDK moving to sandboxes. His advice: models, prompts and even frameworks are easy to swap, so choose where your agent's code runs before you choose a framework.

items.summary: Tapping into the country’s strengths in manufacturing and engineering, NVIDIA is helping advance Korea’s physical AI ecosystem. items.content:
Tapping into the country’s strengths in manufacturing and engineering, NVIDIA is helping advance Korea’s physical AI ecosystem.

The country’s industry leaders are applying accelerated computing, AI and simulation to everything from semiconductor manufacturing to robotics and autonomous vehicles.

These efforts are helping bring physical AI from development into real-world production.

Samsung Advances Semiconductor Engineering With Accelerated Computing and AI Physics

Samsung Electronics is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA to advance semiconductor innovation through accelerated computing and AI physics. The work spans materials research, process development and device engineering.

In technology computer-aided design, Samsung is working with NVIDIA cuISS and NVIDIA cuDSS to accelerate computations involving sparse linear systems. The collaboration also extends to GPU acceleration for process and optical simulations. In materials research, Samsung’s sMOL platform has run selected quantum chemical calculations up to 5x faster end to end with NVIDIA cuEST. Samsung is also exploring NVIDIA cuEquivariance to speed up tensor operations used in training and inference for atomistic AI models.

Samsung is developing chip-scale thermal and mechanical analysis workflows with NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. In one AI homogenization case, combining AI-predicted effective material properties, coarser grids and GPU acceleration resulted in a roughly 1,600x speedup. Simulation time fell from about 18 hours for a fine-grid solve on a 32-core CPU to 41 seconds for a GPU-accelerated coarse-grid solve.

Looking ahead, NVIDIA Agent Toolkit could connect these simulation tools and AI models, helping future engineering agents run analyses and compare design options.

Kakao Mobility Collaborates With NVIDIA to Advance Autonomous Driving Development

Kakao Mobility plans to build on NVIDIA’s autonomous vehicle computing and safety technologies to advance development of a level 4 autonomous driving system. The work combines Kakao Mobility’s proprietary driving software and experience operating in Seoul’s Gangnam district with NVIDIA’s vehicle computing platform.

Kakao Mobility plans to use NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference platform for vehicle sensors and compute, powered by NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor. It also plans to use NVIDIA Halos to support safety across the development and validation of its autonomous driving technology.

Initial development is planned around Kia purpose-built vehicles, integrating Kakao Mobility’s autonomous driving software with NVIDIA technologies. The effort aims to support future level 4 mobility services in Korea.

LG Electronics Advances Robot Learning and Factory Simulation

NVIDIA and LG Electronics successfully demonstrated NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-powered robotic manipulation and manufacturing tasks using LG’s CLOiD robot in an actual manufacturing environment. 

The collaboration implemented a physical AI data flywheel connecting real-world data collection, NVIDIA Cosmos-based data augmentation, GR00T model training, NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor onboard computing and simulation-based evaluation, establishing reusable workflows for continued development and validation of CLOiD’s robotic capabilities. 

The teams are using this work to refine a repeatable process for training, evaluating and improving robots for manufacturing.

items.title: Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA
items.summary: As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them. Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows. A key […]
items.content:
As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them.

Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows.

A key component of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, OpenShell provides a secure runtime with sandboxed execution and policy-based controls to safeguard sensitive data, manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions.

AIM Intelligence, a Korean AI security company, is integrating its Starfort agent control platform with NVIDIA OpenShell. The goal is to combine OpenShell’s runtime access controls with Starfort’s detection of malicious instructions and data leakage. The company is also considering a preliminary proof of concept for the public energy sector, with potential applications across enterprise, industrial and robotics environments.

On the model side, LG AI Research is opening application programming interface access for K-EXAONE-2.5, developed using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets, including Nemotron-Personas-Korea. 

Nemotron-Personas-Korea is an open dataset of 7 million fully synthetic Korean personas, grounded in official Korean statistics, that model builders use to ground training data and evaluation in Korean contexts. NVIDIA Nemotron is a family of open models, datasets and techniques that help developers build specialized, efficient AI agents. 

Learn more about NVIDIA Nemotron open models and get started building secure agents with NVIDIA OpenShell.

items.content:
NVIDIA and Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) are expanding their collaboration across the country’s sovereign AI ecosystem, from AI semiconductors and data center infrastructure to talent, startups, models, agents and security.

The collaboration lays the groundwork for Korean NPU and XPU companies to explore participation in the NVIDIA NVLink Fusion ecosystem, and includes NVIDIA training and certification programs, hackathons and technical seminars to strengthen GPU utilization.

Through Korea’s AI for All initiative, NVIDIA will collaborate with three selected consortia and four leading Korean foundation model builders, using NVIDIA Dynamo software to optimize and scale AI inference.

In addition, NVIDIA today announced a collaboration with SK Telecom and Rebellions, supported by MSIT, to advance sovereign AI infrastructure for Korean models and workloads with NVIDIA NVLink Fusion. Read more in the press release.

As models grow beyond the capacity of a single GPU, they must be split across multiple GPUs, requiring careful coordination of request routing […]
items.content:
NVIDIA is releasing Dynamo-optimized deployment recipes for Korea’s leading open models: A.X K2 from SK Telecom, K-EXAONE 2.0 from LG AI Research, Solar Open 2 from Upstage and Motif-3 from Motif Technologies.

As models grow beyond the capacity of a single GPU, they must be split across multiple GPUs, requiring careful coordination of request routing and communication to maintain performance. 

NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source, distributed inference-serving framework built to deploy models in multi-node environments at data center scale. It handles this routing and communication to maximize inference performance.

Optimized for NVIDIA B200 GPUs, these recipes take the guesswork out of deployment, delivering up to 2x performance out of the box. They help developers bring Korea’s open models into production faster and turn them into broadly accessible AI for All services.

Learn more about NVIDIA Dynamo.
items.author: Amr Elmeleegy

items.title: TATG: Tracking-Aware Testing Objective for LLM-based Test Generation
items.summary:
arXiv:2607.03194v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Complex Java methods challenge automated unit test generation, as achieving high coverage and fault detection requires satisfying intricate testing requirements involving program states, execution paths, and assertions. Existing LLM-based approaches leverage program context, static analysis, and dynamic feedback but lack explicit tracking of individual testing requirements across iterations, potentially leading to redundant generation and unresolved testing objectives.
  We present TATG, a tracking-aware LLM-based unit test generation framework that unifies structural coverage and mutation-based fault detection. TATG introduces a structured objective representation capturing testing requirements derived from static analysis and dynamic feedback, enabling fine-grained tracking of their satisfaction status. It employs a two-stage workflow that first improves structural coverage and subsequently strengthens assertions through mutation-guided hardening.
  We evaluate TATG on 141 complex Java methods against state-of-the-art baselines, including KTester and PANTA. Results show average improvements of 22.15, 20.14, and 37.66 percentage points in line coverage, branch coverage, and mutation score, respectively. TATG also outperforms general-purpose coding assistants, including Codex and Claude Code, under the same open-weight model configurations, achieving higher average coverage and mutation scores while generating fewer tests and consuming fewer tokens. These findings highlight the value of explicitly tracking testing objectives for effective LLM-based test generation.
items.author: Guancheng Wang, Qinghua Xu, Lionel Briand

items.title: Augmentation with Dilution? A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Human Contributor Ecosystems After AI Coding Agent Adoption
items.summary:
arXiv:2606.26289v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI coding agents are rapidly proliferating in open-source software development, and the long-term sustainability of open-source projects is closely tied to the health of their human contributor ecosystems. Yet most existing studies treat human contributors as a static backdrop, and the available evidence on human participation after agent adoption mainly concerns newcomer outcomes. This paper takes the human contributor ecosystem as its dependent variable. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first study to estimate how agent adoption changes the number of distinct humans behind each pull request, and to relate this change to agent pull requests recorded under developer accounts. Using the AIDev dataset, GitHub API scanning, agent-trace screening, and two-stage propensity score matching, we construct a balanced panel of 2,246 treated and 3,798 control repositories from January 2023 to May 2026, and estimate effects with the Sun-Abraham estimator for staggered difference-in-differences, event studies, and HonestDiD sensitivity analysis. AI agent adoption is associated with a decline in human contributor density of 0.019 to 0.048, about 4-10% of its pre-adoption level, depending on the reference month (both p < 0.01); because this estimate tolerates only small violations of parallel trends, we regard it as suggestive evidence. The share of newcomers shows no detectable change (ATT = -0.009, p = 0.28), with the 95% confidence interval ruling out a decrease of more than 2.4 percentage points. Whether the decline in density is associated with agent pull requests recorded under developer accounts remains inconclusive (high minus low share: -0.013, 95% CI [-0.083, 0.057]). These findings are consistent with a pattern of augmentation with dilution: we detect no decrease in the share of newcomers, but each human contributor appears to correspond to more pull requests.
items.author: Weixing Zhang, Bowen Jiang, Tianhai Liu, Jialong Li, Anne Koziolek

items.title: Cloud-OpsBench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Agentic Root Cause Analysis in Cloud Systems
items.summary:
arXiv:2603.00468v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: LLM agents are explored for automating root cause analysis (RCA) in cloud-native systems, creating a need to evaluate both diagnostic correctness and the quality of the supporting investigation. Existing static benchmarks offer repeatable inputs but limited system-facing interaction, while live testbeds expose tools but hinder controlled comparison because incident evidence varies across runs; both paradigms focus primarily on final answers. To address these limitations, we present Cloud-OpsBench, an evaluation infrastructure for interactive and evidence-grounded cloud RCA. It comprises 754 runtime-verified cases across 57 fault types on two microservice workloads spanning application services and Kubernetes platform layers. Each fault is captured as a state snapshot and replayed through standard diagnostic interfaces, with outcome labels and diagnostic evidence graphs that enable matched comparisons and process-level analysis. Evaluating eleven LLMs on Cloud-OpsBench reveals that strong outcome accuracy often masks incomplete investigations: while Joint RCA Accuracy (JRA) reaches up to 0.78 on OnlineBoutique and 0.68 on TrainTicket, models identify the correct root cause without achieving evidence closure (e.g., in 33.1% and 29.4% of evaluated cases for GPT-5). These results demonstrate that final-answer accuracy alone cannot establish whether an agent has traced the failure and collected the evidence needed to confirm its root cause.
items.author: Yilun Wang, Guangba Yu, Haiyu Huang, Yujie Huang, Zirui Wang, Pengfei Chen, Michael R. Lyu

items.title: OmniLink: Specification-Based Trace Validation of Concurrent Systems with Substep Linearizability
items.summary:
arXiv:2601.11836v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Concurrent systems are notoriously difficult to validate. We present OmniLink, a methodology for validating traces of concurrent implementations against high-level specifications in TLA+. Unlike prior TLA+ based approaches, OmniLink treats system events as black boxes with a timebox in which they occurred and a meaning in TLA+, solving for a logical total order of actions. Unlike prior approaches based on linearizability checking, OmniLink implements substep linearizability semantics, relies on a flexible specification language, accelerates checking with user-customizable path pruning specifications, and can detect violations due to weak memory effects between operations. Our evaluation validates WiredTiger, a state-of-the-art industrial database storage layer; Balanced Augmented Tree (BAT), a state-of-the art lock-free data structure from the research community; and, ConcurrentQueue, a popular lock-free queue featuring aggressive performance optimizations. OmniLink detects injected and previously fixed bugs in the systems under test. It also uncovers a previously unknown bug in BAT that has been confirmed by its authors.
items.author: Finn Hackett, Evan Wrench, Peter Macko, A. Jesse Jiryu Davis, Yuanhao Wei, Ivan Beschastnikh

items.title: Strategic Competition and Convergence in LLM Leaderboards
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.09780v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Leaderboards are a popular way to compare large language model (LLM) capabilities and can influence how model developers invest resources. We ask when competition on leaderboards leads developers to produce models with similar capability profiles, which we call monoculture, or similar performance levels. We study this by formulating leaderboard competition as a game in which model developers invest resources across capabilities to maximize their win rate. We show that similar production functions can induce similar capability profiles, while comparative advantage can sustain distinct capability profiles. We then study convergence in performance levels and show that diminishing returns can lead to an increasingly crowded competitive frontier. Using data from LM Arena and OpenRouter, we find that developers improve more in categories where they lag competitors, while still retaining category-specific advantages. At the same time, we find that the frontier of models becomes increasingly crowded, alongside increasingly diversified model usage patterns. Our results suggest that increasing competition does not need to produce interchangeable models, but can instead sustain competitive models with distinct strengths.
items.author: Naveen Raman, Fei Fang, Yiling Chen

items.title: TwinLight: A Multi-Timescale Physical-Layer-Aware T-API-Compliant Optical Domain Controller Digital Twin
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.09359v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We demonstrate TwinLight, an open-source optical-network digital twin acting as an optical domain controller. Its T-API REST and telemetry streaming interfaces expose a physical-layer engine that combines a GNPy steady-state baseline with four analytical transients.
items.author: Carlos Natalino, Piotr Lechowicz, Renato Ambrosone, Enrico Miotto, Vittorio Curri, Paolo Monti

items.title: National and State-Level Approaches to Automated Vehicle Certification: A Comparative Framework for State Operational Governance
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.08681v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Automated vehicle (AV) deployment in the United States is expanding without a unified federal certification framework, leading to substantial variation in how states authorize and oversee AV testing and deployment. This paper examines how U.S. states regulate Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) Level 4-5 automated driving systems (ADS), identifies common certification approaches, compares them with international practices, and evaluates the implications for North Carolina's future regulatory strategy. Publicly available state statutes, administrative regulations, agency guidance, and federal policy documents were reviewed. Ten states, selected to capture the range of regulatory approaches, were analyzed using a structured framework covering operational scope, governance and oversight, federal interaction, and implementation outcomes. Certification practices in the European Union, China, Japan, and Australia were reviewed for comparative context. Three state certification models were identified, reflecting increasing regulatory involvement: baseline legal compliance, administrative self-certification with ongoing oversight, and permit-based authorization requiring formal agency review before deployment. North Carolina currently aligns with the baseline compliance model. International frameworks are converging toward scenario-based testing, operational-design-domain-specific approval, safety-case documentation, cybersecurity assurance, and lifecycle oversight, although direct transferability to the U.S. is limited. The paper develops a three-model typology for comparing state AV certification approaches and integrates state practices with international frameworks, providing a consistent basis for evaluating differences in regulatory involvement, governance complexity, and institutional responsibilities across jurisdictions.
items.author: Sk Nahia Ahsan, Md Abdullah Al Hasan, Danjue Chen, George List

items.title: Aegis OS: A Transactional Multi-Tenant Operating System Runtime for Eliminating Authorization Fatigue in Autonomous Coding Agents
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.08516v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Autonomous coding agents such as Google Antigravity (agy), Anthropic Claude Code (claude), and OpenAI Codex CLI (codex) execute multi-step software engineering workflows on workstations and cloud hosts. Existing agent environments face a Security-Autonomy Dilemma: operators must choose between per-action confirmation prompts, which interrupt workflows on 45%-57% of tool calls and induce authorization fatigue, or unconfined execution (--yolo / --dangerously-skip-permissions), which exposes host files, SSH/cloud credentials, and API tokens to prompt injection and hallucination risks. Furthermore, concurrent agents editing a shared working tree clobber one another's changes, while passing large artifacts inline through LLM context windows incurs high token overhead.
  We present Aegis OS (aegis-os), a transactional, multi-tenant Agent Operating System Runtime in Rust exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol. Aegis OS shifts the authorization boundary from individual tool calls to transactional workspace boundaries. Each agent runs inside a kernel-enforced OS sandbox (macOS Seatbelt and Linux Bubblewrap with default-deny --tmpfs $HOME isolation and a Unix-socket egress bridge) backed by a Copy-on-Write (CoW) shadow workspace (APFS clonefile; single-open Linux FICLONE reflinks), an identity-pinned HTTP Egress Proxy with L7 method/path-scoped secret injection and outbound DLP, and an A2A IPC bus with Content-Addressable Storage (CAS). Across 1,500 controlled calls and 28,087 real calls across 52 coding-agent sessions, Aegis OS reduces prompts by 94.19%-99.88% (controlled) and 90.7%-97.9% (real sessions, 1.12% IPR), lowers attack success rate across 80 attacks in eight categories from 100.0% to 0.0% on macOS and Linux, clones 1,000-file (78.1 MB) repos in 6.3 ms on APFS and 15.6 ms on btrfs, and catches 10/10 syntactic and semantic merge conflicts.
items.author: Hui Zhao (Heurion Research)

items.title: Literature Review of Mixed Reality Research
items.summary:
arXiv:2312.02995v2 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: In the global context, while mixed reality has been an emerging concept for years, recent technological and scientific advancements have now made it poised to revolutionize industries and daily life by offering enhanced functionalities and improved services. Besides reviewing the highly cited papers in the last 20 years among over a thousand research papers on mixed reality, this systematic review provides the state-of-the-art applications and utilities of the mixed reality by primarily scrutinizing the associated papers in 2022 and 2023. Focusing on the potentials that this technology have in providing digitally supported simulations and other utilities in the era of large language models, highlighting the potential and limitations of the innovative solutions and also bringing focus to emerging research directions, such as telemedicine, remote control and optimization of direct volume rendering. The paper's associated repository is publicly accessible at https://aizierjiang.github.io/mr.
items.author: Aizierjiang Aiersilan

items.title: An Empirical Study on Clustering-based Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for Regression Test Case Selection
items.summary:
arXiv:2611.09869v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Regression testing assesses whether software components that have already been developed and tested continue to work correctly after modifications.
