items.title: How NVIDIA Open Source Tools Are Helping Researchers Build Next-Generation 6G Networks
items.summary: A year ago, NVIDIA open sourced its Aerial wireless software, joining Sionna and a broader suite of open source tools for accelerating next-generation 6G network development. Together, they give researchers a foundation for testing ideas, comparing results and building on each other’s work — connecting simulation and AI training with experiments on real over-the-air wireless […]
items.content:
A year ago, NVIDIA open sourced its Aerial wireless software, joining Sionna and a broader suite of open source tools for accelerating next-generation 6G network development. Together, they give researchers a foundation for testing ideas, comparing results and building on each other’s work — connecting simulation and AI training with experiments on real over-the-air wireless systems.

Today, researchers and developers are using these tools to build 6G-ready networks that do more than just transmit data — receiving signals more effectively, keeping robots and autonomous systems connected when it matters most, and adapting in real time as devices move through the world.

Over the past year, global developer adoption of NVIDIA AI Aerial and NVIDIA Sionna software has grown 10x, while NVIDIA’s open source 5G/6G tools have surpassed 1 million downloads. More than 8,000 research and academic institutions worldwide are using these platforms. 

The projects emerging today offer a view of how future networks could look. Each addresses a different challenge, but together point toward a broader ambition for building AI-native 6G networks that deliver connectivity, computing and sensing over a converged software-defined platform for billions of people, machines and agents.

Networks That Help Robots React Faster

A robot picking up an object needs to understand its surroundings and act before they change. When the AI powering that decision runs on a nearby server or in the cloud, the wireless connection becomes part of the response time. 

Researchers are exploring a more efficient approach called goal-oriented semantic communications. Instead of sending full images, robots transmit compact descriptions of objects, their positions and their relationships. Transmitting just as much information as needed allows robots to more quickly respond, especially in dynamic environments like workplaces and warehouses.

At King’s College London, researchers connected a camera-equipped robot arm to an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin running NVIDIA Sionna, which supports both software-defined 5G network and edge AI processing. In fruit-packing and cube-stacking experiments with deliberately introduced faults, the approach reduced robot task completion time by up to 52.6% and improved task success compared with sending periodic images.

In addition to quicker responses and less processing overhead, the system also proved more resilient — detecting dropped objects, recovering from unsuccessful actions and, in configurations using a digital twin, checking planned movements for potential collisions before execution. 

Networks That Learn to Receive Signals Better

For a firefighter receiving live drone footage or a rescue team searching for a missing person, timely images can help guide urgent decisions. But interference and changing radio conditions can make wireless signals harder to decode, causing errors and retransmissions that delay information from the field.

AI receivers address this challenge by learning to recover information from incoming signals more effectively. Better reception could help responders maintain a clearer, more current view of a fire scene or search area.

SoftBank demonstrated this by integrating a neural receiver into NVIDIA Aerial CUDA-Accelerated RAN (ACAR) and testing it with a commercial 5G smartphone. In controlled tests with interference, the neural receiver delivered higher uplink throughput than a conventional receiver at all 15 tested settings, with a maximum gain of roughly 60%.

Another way to improve reception is to teach receivers about the environments where they operate. Using NVIDIA Aerial Testbed, ETH Zurich researchers found that tuning neural receivers using local measurements reduced block error rates by more than one-third compared with selected pretrained versions. 

Networks That Learn When to Save Power

As 6G connects more devices and supports more AI applications, managing energy demand will become increasingly important. 

For example, a network may need enough capacity to serve a busy stadium, but demand changes when the crowd leaves. AI can help identify when spare capacity can power down — and when it needs to come back online — so operators can reduce electricity use without dropping connections.

At the University of Leeds, researchers developed a system that predicts network demand 10 minutes ahead and uses those forecasts to guide base station sleep decisions. Before powering down, it checks that neighboring active stations can continue serving affected devices and monitors for changes that require capacity to be restored.

The team tested their approach using a portable, NVIDIA DGX Spark-powered 5G “network-in-a-box” alongside a digital twin for validating decisions against real wireless equipment. The result: researchers reported a 45.6% reduction in RAN power consumption relative to a full-power baseline while maintaining device connectivity.

Networks That Can Be Tested Faster — Before They’re Built

Before deploying a network, researchers need to know how it will perform when hundreds of devices compete for connections or radio signals run into interference. Simulating these conditions helps teams evaluate designs before committing to costly equipment and field trials. But realistic simulations can take hours, limiting how many ideas researchers can explore.

The Centre Tecnològic de Telecomunicacions de Catalunya (CTTC) is accelerating that process by bringing GPU-accelerated radio channel models, running on ACAR, into CTTC’s open source 5G-LENA network simulator. These models calculate how wireless signals travel between antennas and devices — a computation that grows increasingly demanding as simulated networks grow.

In an early evaluation, the approach reduced simulation runtime from approximately three hours to 10-20 minutes, depending on the integration, while preserving the expected statistical behavior and network performance.

Faster simulations let researchers compare more designs, investigate more demanding scenarios and refine ideas sooner. As the industry develops 6G, this could shorten the path from a proposed innovation to a thoroughly evaluated network design — helping teams build better connectivity before deploying it in the real world.

At NVIDIA GTC Washington, D.C., attend 6G Developer Sessions where researchers and developers will showcase more innovations shaping the future of wireless networks. 

NVIDIA AI Aerial and NVIDIA Sionna are available on GitHub.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

Vera Delivers the Best of Both Worlds: Highest Throughput and Fastest Agents
items.summary: AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action.  Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task.  As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those […]
items.content:
AI agents do more than generate answers. They search for information, query databases, write and test code and take action. 

Each of those steps relies on a CPU, with agents moving between GPU reasoning and CPU execution throughout a task. 

As businesses put more agents to work, AI factories need CPUs that can execute those steps quickly and support many agents at once, all within the limits of available power.

What this means: AI infrastructure providers need to support more agents without making each one wait longer to get work done. And critically, AI factories are power limited. This means operators need to choose infrastructure that maximizes the work done for every watt. 

Why it matters: NVIDIA Vera delivers both fast agent performance and high capacity per watt within a single CPU. That gives providers one CPU for a range of agent workloads, rather than having to mix and match fast and dense x86 parts to balance speed and capacity.

The data that proves it: In a 100-megawatt data center comparison, NVIDIA found that a single Vera CPU performs better than the fastest x86 CPU and the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.

  • Vera delivers industry-leading agent speed while enabling 1.6x more agents per watt versus the fastest x86 CPU.
  • Vera delivers 2x faster agent speed with leading energy efficiency compared with the most energy-efficient x86 CPU.

Partners are already putting Vera to work. Early adopters see the same exceptional performance in production-style tests:

  • Perplexity: Ran agentic coding tasks 1.5x faster with Vera than on traditional CPUs. Perplexity plans to deploy Vera in an upcoming production system.
  • DeepInfra: Delivered up to 2.2x speed of the best x86 processor on agentic orchestration for its production agent workload, achieving the fastest of the four architectures tested.
  • ClickHouse: Its standard binary, with no Vera-specific tuning, scaled near-linearly across 176 cores and topped the ClickBench hardware leaderboard.
  • DuckLabs: Achieved about 1.5x the median TPC-H SF1000 performance of an Intel Xeon 6 baseline.
  • Daytona: Brought 1,000 agent sandboxes online in 10.8 seconds, and achieved 12.7 completed jobs per second at 2,000 concurrent sandboxes, using Vera versus 88.4 seconds with x86.
  • Modal: Achieved up to 2x sandbox throughput per core versus comparable x86 hardware, with gains that grow under heavy load.

Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera CPU.

items.title: Agents Are Going Async
items.summary:
• As agents take on bigger goals, they need to stay responsive to the user while making progress on many long tasks at once.
  • Async subagents split an agent into an orchestrator that stays available to the user and subagents that run tasks in the background and report back to the orchestrator upon completion.
  • Background work is becoming the norm for agent infrastructure, from coding agents like Claude Code to personal agents like OpenAI's dots.

Imagine a chief of staff who disappears every time you hand them a big project and only comes back once it's done. You'd probably fire them immediately. A good chief of staff keeps projects moving in the background while staying reachable and keeping you updated along the way. As we ask agents to work toward bigger goals, they need the same two properties. An agent has to be responsive, acting on a new instruction right away with the context of everything before it, and productive, making progress on many large tasks at once.

The architecture we've used to build agents for a while can't meet both requirements. In a standard ReAct loop, each long tool call blocks the loop and every other task queues behind it. Instead, we're seeing the ecosystem converge on a split between one agent that stays with the user and background workers that do the long work. Claude Code runs subagents in the background by default, OpenAI's dots hand work to background workers to make progress on several things at once, and DeepSeek Harness built its super agent around a router that talks to people and background workers that run tasks in parallel.

We’re bringing this pattern to Deep Agents with async subagents. An orchestrator stays available to the user and keeps the conversation's context organized, while async subagents run as background workers and report back when they finish. The amount of work the agent can take on then grows with the number of background workers instead of the length of one loop.

How async subagents work

An agent runs in a loop. The model calls a tool, waits for the result, and decides what to do next. Historically, tools and subagents blocked that loop until they returned, like code that awaits each slow call in turn. An async subagent works like a task started with asyncio.create_task or a Promise you don't await yet. The call returns right away, the work runs independently in the background, and the result comes back later.

Async work depends on two properties of the system:

  • The user can reach the orchestrator. The orchestrator is the agent the user interacts directly with. Subagents no longer hold its loop, so the user can reach it whenever its own loop isn't busy, instead of waiting for every subagent to finish.
  • Tasks run in parallel without blocking. The orchestrator starts subagents as work comes in, instead of waiting for a whole batch to return.

The orchestrator manages async subagents with five tools:

  • start_async_task starts a subagent on its own thread and returns right away.
  • check_async_task gets a task's status and, once it finishes, its result.
  • update_async_task sends a running task new instructions.
  • cancel_async_task stops a running task.
  • list_async_tasks lists every task and its status.

Steering a running subagent is separate from reaching the orchestrator. When the orchestrator sends a follow-up with update_async_task, the update_strategy field on that subagent's definition decides what happens:

  • "interrupt" (the default) stops the current run and restarts the subagent with the new instruction. Use it for a correction like "use Postgres instead."
  • "enqueue" holds the follow-up until the current run finishes. Use it for an addition like "run the tests when you're done."

How notifications work

Every unfinished task is listed in the orchestrator's system prompt, so it always knows what's in flight. It can poll with check_async_task or tasks can report back on their own:

  • If the orchestrator is busy, it checks its unfinished tasks before each model call and picks up the result mid-run.
  • If it's idle, the subagent wakes it with a new run.
  • If it's paused on an approval, the approval is left alone, and the result arrives once the user answers.

A subagent that needs approval shows up as waiting, and the user answers on the subagent's own thread without interrupting the orchestrator. In Managed Deep Agents on Slack, the request posts back to the original thread.

We expect this pattern to generalize beyond subagents to tools across the board. OpenAI recently added support for async tool calling, where the model keeps working after it calls a tool and your application sends the result back in a later request.

Use async subagents

Async subagents are available in Deep Agents for Python and JavaScript, and in Managed Deep Agents, where making a subagent async takes one field:

from managed_deepagents import define_deep_agent

agent = define_deep_agent(
    name="research-assistant",
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    subagents=[
        {
            "name": "researcher",
            "description": "Researches a topic in the background.",
            "system_prompt": "Research the topic and report your findings.",
            "async": True,
        },
    ],
)

In Managed Deep Agents, every served agent also gets an async copy of the general-purpose subagent, so it can decide at runtime whether to run delegated work in the foreground or the background.

Task notifications are in beta, so the API may still change. The async-deep-agents repo has a working supervisor with researcher and coder subagents in Python and TypeScript.

Give async subagents a try, and let us know what you think in GitHub issues or on the forum.

Into the Omniverse: How Developers Turn Ideas Into Simulations With Frontier AI Agents
items.summary: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs. Developers direct AI agents through […]
items.content:
Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.

Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.

Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.

 

Create Editable 3D Assets With Houdini and AI Agents

Creating animated 3D content requires connecting modeling, simulation, materials and rendering. Nick Scarcella, a senior technical artist on NVIDIA’s BondLab team, directed AI agents — primarily using Claude — to work with CUDA libraries and Isaac Sim to create animations. The BondLab team uses SideFX Houdini and the NVIDIA ovrtx library to develop materials, lighting and the final rendered appearance.

In one experiment, Scarcella guided Astra to recreate an OP-1 portable synthesizer using product images, manuals and technical direction. He exported the model into the OpenUSD framework, tested it in Houdini and Blender, then used Astra and Opus to refine details before adjusting materials and textures for ovrtx rendering.

Scarcella also used a publicly shared robot-hand checkpoint in Isaac Sim, directing the motion and developing materials and lighting in Houdini with Claude’s assistance. Working with team member Steven Dvornik, the team created an “Echos” visualization: translucent versions of the hand overlap and merge into a single hand animation, offering a visual interpretation of robot training.

Figure: An artistic visualization of simulated robot-hand motion, developed with AI assistance and Houdini’s materials and lighting tools.

These workflows bring agent-assisted creation into existing artist tools, giving teams editable content they can inspect, refine and render across applications.

Explore Scarcella’s Houdini MCP tools and agent skill.

 

Test Robotic Disassembly With Computer-Aided Design and Simulation

Before a robot can disassemble a product, developers need to know whether its tools can reach and remove the parts. Jens Jebens, a senior product manager for OpenUSD at NVIDIA, directed Astra to model a car suspension in PTC Onshape and configure it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

Jebens used simulation feedback to revise the tooling, including a wrench designed to reach the suspension’s bolts, and reported successful removal of a suspension component in simulation.

 

PTC also connects computer-aided design (CAD) with simulation through Onshape’s SimReady Publisher, built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Robotics startup Sensori uses it to transfer its Yuri robot into Isaac Sim, carrying geometry, joints and configuration data so the team can evaluate design changes without repeatedly rebuilding the simulation model.

Read Sensori’s story.

Explore the Onshape importer guide.

 

Create an Editable Building Model From Site Scans

 

Planning warehouse automation requires a model of the building itself, but shelving and machinery can obscure its structure in site scans. Omniverse brings together real-to-sim tools and agent skills to help developers turn real-world captures into editable starting environments for physical AI simulation.

David Wehr, from NVIDIA’s simulation technology team, built on that work using Astra to develop a workflow for digitally reconstructing a building without its contents. The goal is an editable, simulation-ready building model where developers can add or reposition shelving and machinery to evaluate warehouse layouts and automation plans before making physical changes.

Wehr guided Astra to interpret panoramic photos, create building geometry and align it with point-cloud measurements. OpenUSD stores the models, while Omniverse’s ovrtx library renders results for inspection.

Explore NVIDIA Omniverse agent skills to help agents build with Omniverse libraries.

 

Test Gas-Turbine Operating Scenarios With a Digital Twin

 

Before changing how industrial equipment operates, engineers need a way to explore the consequences. Pradeep Kaushik, a member of the NVIDIA Omniverse developer relations team, directed Astra to build a what-if analysis application around a simulated gas turbine and generator.

The application lets users adjust conditions such as load, ambient temperature and fuel composition, then compare power, efficiency, fuel consumption and equipment response. Six test procedures explore scenarios including load changes, a stuck fuel valve and an exhaust-sensor error.

The prototype gives engineers an interactive way to investigate how operating changes and faults could affect equipment behavior, supporting decisions about which scenarios warrant further testing.

Astra used tools like Cantera for thermochemistry and SciPy for equipment dynamics. The application maps solver results to rotor animation and color-coded temperature, pressure and flow-velocity indicators in a 3D turbine. NVIDIA Omniverse libraries update the scene (ovstage), render it with RTX (ovrtx) and stream the view to the browser (ovstream). Engineers can rotate and zoom the cutaway, switch between indicators, and pause or scrub through a simulated response alongside charts and virtual instruments.

 

Build Simulation Scenes With Open Source SimReady Assets

 

With SimReady Central Library, announced at GTC Berlin, developers can access more than 2,000 simulation-ready USD assets from equipment manufacturers and asset providers for robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins workflows.

Paul Kind, a member of NVIDIA’s Omniverse documentation team, pointed an AI agent to the library and guided scene assembly through conversation. His kitchen scene included 180 placements drawn from 63 unique library assets, alongside 18 custom geometry pieces. Kind reviewed renders produced with Isaac Sim and guided further adjustments.

For robotics and factory workflows, developers can select SimReady assets with the simulation properties embedded to fit their required task then test in an assembled environment.

Find assets in SimReady Central Library, and learn how to contribute.

 

Stress-Test a Warehouse Simulation at Scale

 

A warehouse simulation needs to keep running smoothly as more robot arms, conveyors and boxes fill the scene.

When it slows down, developers need to identify what’s holding it back. Bhavik Sanganee, principal engineer at NVIDIA, used Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to build a warehouse simulation, increase its complexity and investigate slowdowns.

Performance first fell below the target when the scene doubled in size. Running physics calculations, image rendering and video preparation concurrently restored performance and enabled further scaling.

With 80 conveyors, 40 arms and 800 boxes, the simulation sustained 30 frames per second at full HD resolution during a two-minute test. The arms completed 640 successful box placements.

Doubling the scene again reduced performance. Testing traced the slowdown to the physics and robot-control pipeline, giving Sanganee a specific area to improve.

Start building with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.

 

Test Robot Control for Flexible Cable Routing

 

In electronics assembly, a robot may need to position a flexible cable around components before plugging it into a port. The cable bends as the robot moves it, and the connector must line up precisely to fit.

Oyindamola Omotuyi, robotics technical marketing manager at NVIDIA, directed Astra to build a robot simulation using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Newton physics and Omniverse rendering with a Robotiq gripper handling the cable.

Astra also developed a reinforcement learning system that combined learned cable-routing movements with position-and-orientation feedback and corrective adjustments for USB-C insertion. The simulation gave Omotuyi a way to test cable handling and connector alignment before moving to physical-robot experiments.

The controller used information supplied directly by the simulation. Next steps include testing a friction-held grasp and using information a physical robot could obtain from cameras and sensors.

Get started with robot learning in NVIDIA Isaac Lab.

 

Turn Robot Computer-Aided Design Into a SimReady Asset

Before testing whether a robot can pick up and move a box, developers need a simulation model with joints that move correctly and with grippers that can hold the object. A computer-aided design (CAD) model provides the robot’s shape, but it still needs physics properties to perform the task.

Using an ABB Robotics YuMi robot, developers directed Astra with NVIDIA Omniverse content libraries to convert CAD files into OpenUSD, match the robot’s appearance to reference images, and configure joints and collision geometry. They checked the asset against SimReady Foundation requirements before testing it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.

Both arms and grippers completed four cube pick-and-place cycles, using simulated finger contact and friction. These tests demonstrated behavior under the simulated conditions — estimated physical properties were not calibrated against the real robot.

Follow the five-step SimReady tutorial. 

 

Build a Humanoid Simulator for a Warehouse Environment

Explore a gamified, physics-based control of a humanoid robot in first- and third-person view.

Before automating warehouse tasks, developers need an interactive simulation environment to explore task behavior and evaluate how the work gets done. Frank DeLise, Omniverse product manager at NVIDIA, used Astra to turn a SimReady warehouse and humanoid robot into an interactive simulator with first- and third-person views.

DeLise directed Astra to connect NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for physics (ovphysx), scene updates (ovstage), rendering (ovrtx) and the user interface (ovui). He also used Astra with SimReady (simready-foundation) to create the physical scene in simulation. Astra then generated animation and application code to bring those capabilities together.

Learn how to prepare and validate SimReady robot assets with frontier AI models and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.

 

Connect an Autonomous-Driving Testing Workflow

 

Changing a scene, sensor or driving model can significantly affect autonomous-vehicle simulations. Doyub Kim, a manager on the simulation technology team at NVIDIA, asked Astra to build Zero to Alpamayo — a reusable simulation environment based on San Francisco’s Market Street.

Kim directed Astra to map out the workflow, then connect asset creation, traffic, Omniverse RTX sensor simulation and Alpamayo driving in stages, checking each integration. The resulting prototype was a testing ground for comparing models and tracing how scene or sensor changes affect downstream driving behavior. A separate Cosmos3-Nano experiment varied weather and lighting in recorded simulation videos, allowing Kim to compare the driving model’s responses to the same scenario under different conditions.

 

Use Sensor Differences to Create and Improve Digital Twins

Comparing recorded and simulated camera and lidar outputs gives developers key performance indicator-based feedback for refining a scene.

To test robots and autonomous vehicles, developers need to know how closely simulated sensors match real ones. Ashley Reid, who works on RTX sensor validation at NVIDIA, directed Astra and Claude Fable 5 agents to compare ovrtx camera and raw LiDAR outputs with recorded data. The agents created two digital twins from scratch and improved two existing ones.

Over about three days, Reid guided an iterative workflow in which agents measured differences, created or modified OpenUSD scenes, and checked the results. Changes addressed missing objects, geometry and materials, with acceptance depending on camera and LiDAR metrics. This gives developers a way to use measured discrepancies to guide scene creation and improvement.

Start by rendering an OpenUSD scene with the ovrtx minimal Python example, then define a sensor measure to compare with recorded data.

 

Robo Olympics: Test Robot Skills With Simulation

Teaching robots new movements means checking whether those actions work under physical constraints. Tae Kim, who leads NVIDIA Omniverse engineering and product, used sports videos and natural-language instructions to guide Astra in building Robo Olympics, an experimental project that tests simulated Unitree G1 humanoids performing sports movements.

Under Kim’s direction, Astra built controllers and refined them through physics trials. Newton Physics Engine simulated behavior, the open source NVIDIA Warp framework accelerated calculations and ovrtx rendered scenes and virtual-camera images. In one experiment, the robot cleared a single hurdle in 64 of 100 simulation trials. The trials gave Kim feedback for improving the robot’s timing and control.

Watch Kim explore building simulations with Astra and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries.

 

Bring the International Space Station Into the Browser

Turning 3D models into an application requires connecting assets, live data and an interface. Nic Johns, an engineering director at NVIDIA, prompted Astra to assemble NASA assets into an OpenUSD International Space Station model with telemetry. Johns built the application with a single prompt, then used a follow-up prompt to shift the scene to Earth’s daytime side so the planet was visible.

The workflow used Blender for asset preparation and Omniverse libraries for rendering (ovrtx), scene runtime (ovstage) and streaming (ovstream). The application brings 3D models and operational data into the browser, with Johns guiding its development through prompts and corrections.

Try the Omniverse Real-Time Viewer skill.

 

Turn Captured Rooms Into Testing Environments

A digitally reconstructed room needs editable objects and accurate physical behavior before developers can test interactions. Chirag Majithia, from the Isaac engineering applications team at NVIDIA, directed Astra to turn stereo camera captures into an editable OpenUSD studio.

The workflow combined PyCuSFM, FoundationStereo and nvblox for reconstruction, with user review guiding object selection and placement. Astra assembled generated and Blender-authored assets and used USD Content Agents to configure how objects move and interact in simulation. Isaac Sim tests guided collision and contact revisions for doors and drawers. The studio connects captured geometry to interaction testing, making gaps and object behavior easier to inspect. 

Explore USD Content Agents.

Have a simulation idea? Explore NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to start building with an AI agent.

items.title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
items.summary: Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers.  […]
items.content:
Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it.

“We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers. 

Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube, where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents. 

“I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.”

Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere

Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it.

“Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.”

That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents.

“I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.”

 

It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand. 

It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains.

“You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.”

In non-wizard terms?

“There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks.

“I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.”

From Birding to Model-Building

Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada.

“After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions.

“Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.”

Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community. 

“To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.”

And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan?

“It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.”

Hear more from Alexiuk by following the NVIDIA Nemotron Labs Livestreams series on YouTube.

items.title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge
items.summary: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack.  […]
items.content:
Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term.

NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack. 

But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory.

That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit. 

How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed. 

Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX.

Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM

Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training.

KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time. 

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain. 

During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM. 

Why AI Factories Need a Memory Hierarchy 

Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move. 

Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. A larger warehouse holds more inventory, but the docks set how much can move in and out at a time. Once the docks are at capacity, moving more inventory takes longer and slows response times. If delays exceed the required service level, the added space can’t be used effectively, even as it adds cost and draws power. 

That’s also why no operation keeps all its inventory in the closest, fastest space. What’s in motion stays near the line. What’s waiting moves to a larger, cheaper space nearby and returns before it’s needed. 

An AI factory faces the same limit. 

More HBM can hold more KV cache and support more concurrent users. Every added user shares the same compute and memory bandwidth. But when each user expects fast responses, eventually memory bandwidth is unable to supply data as fast as compute can use it: a limit engineers call the memory wall. 

Past that point, extra HBM capacity can’t be put to work, yet it still adds costs and draws power. The data still needs a place to live, but not all of it needs the fastest, most expensive tier. This is why an AI factory manages data across a memory and storage hierarchy. 

Maximizing the Value of Every Byte With Full-Stack Codesign

NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign makes every byte of HBM count by relieving pressure from model weights, KV cache and RAG data. It does this with techniques that each target a different source of inefficiency: 

Shrink model weights and distribute them across the NVL72 domain.

  • The NVFP4 format reduces the space required for weights compared to FP8, the lowest precision possible on the NVIDIA Hopper platform. Recent models, including FLUX.2 [klein] from Black Forest Labs, Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab, Beam 1.0 from Reflection, Meta Muse Spark from Meta, Step 5 Preview from StepFun and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL have been released with NVFP4 checkpoints, demonstrating growing model-builder adoption of 4-bit precision for faster, more memory-efficient inference. 
  • Within an NVL72 system, model weights can be distributed across up to 72 GPUs, so each GPU holds a smaller share of the model — leaving more HBM for KV cache and concurrent users. 

Shrink KV-cache and offload inactive context to lower-cost storage tiers.

  • Applying NVFP4 to the KV cache reduces its footprint compared with FP8, so more context can stay resident in HBM.
  • NVIDIA Vera CPU helps in two ways. Faster tool execution shortens the time KV cache sits inactive during tool calls, and its large LPDDR memory, connected to NVIDIA Rubin GPUs over NVIDIA NVLink-C2C interconnect, gives paused context a nearby place to wait and return quickly. 
  • When context isn’t actively in use, NVIDIA Dynamo inference software moves it to NVIDIA CMX context memory storage — a tier built for capacity at far lower cost per bit than HBM — and returns it before reuse. Unlike local SSDs, CMX is shared across servers, and unlike enterprise storage, it skips the overhead of long-term data protection that short-lived context doesn’t need. NVIDIA CMX context memory storage partners include Cloudian, DDN, Dell Technologies, Everpure (previously Pure Storage), HPE, IBM, NetApp, VAST and WEKA. 
  • Dynamo’s KV Cache Reuse ties the tiers together, managing KV cache as one system-wide resource across GPU memory, CPU memory and storage, so context computed once can be reused across the system. 

Compact RAG embeddings and keeping the index outside HBM.

  • RAG turns enterprise documents into embeddings — numerical representations that let a system search by meaning rather than keyword — organized into a searchable index. NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models produce smaller embeddings with higher retrieval accuracy, while the NVIDIA cuVS library enables that index to be built and served across CPU and storage. The knowledge base never occupies HBM, and only the passages the model needs enter context. 

The result is less HBM used for model weights, less HBM tied up by idle context and more of it available to serve concurrent users. 

More Useful Output per Dollar With Each Generation

Across successive NVIDIA platform generations, tokens per second per dollar has risen far faster than HBM capacity. 

On the SemiAnalysis AgentX DeepSeek V4 Pro workload, NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 delivers up to 10x higher throughput per dollar than NVIDIA H200 platform at 100 tokens per second per user, with HBM capacity per GPU roughly doubling. At 125 tokens per second per user, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 30x higher throughput per dollar than GB300 NVL72, with HBM capacity per GPU up about 3%. 

For AI factory operators, the metric that matters is how many useful tokens the factory can deliver within its power budget while meeting user response-time needs. More tokens per second per watt means more work and revenue from the same power, and a lower cost for every token. NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign lowers token costs by increasing the useful work every byte of memory delivers. 

Learn more in the video explainer and technical deep dive on how NVIDIA full-stack codesign reduces inference memory pressure.

items.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
items.summary:
AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line.

The post Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit appeared first on Microsoft Research.
items.content:
At a glance

  • Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here.
  • Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. 
  • PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab), proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach.
  • We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab), we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. 

The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it.

Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. 

This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up.

So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in.

Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical.

Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it.

How PDD Kit works

PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab), GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document.

The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact, a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. 

Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: 

  • Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab), a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science.
  • Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof.

The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB): the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. 

The capstone: a full-stack web app

To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab). The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab). Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust.

For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: 

Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements:

  1. You only get a token with the right password.
  2. Only admin accounts get admin tokens.

We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job.

Step 1: Questions before code

PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. 

The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways.

Step 2: A human readable intent map

As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3).

Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent.

The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token.

Step 3: Proving the login function

Before anything gets built, PDD Kit asks the team to sign off on the plan as a whole. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6).

That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow, carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. 

Step 4: Where proof stops

There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them:

  • Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. 
  • Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. 
  • Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. 
  • Anything a person has to judge, like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. 
  • Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. 

That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification, asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces:

  • The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username. Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. 
  • check_password, a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify. It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. 
  • generate_token, which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. 
  • expiry_from_now, which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. 
  • database_error, which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. 
  • The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. 

In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification:

/// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. 
#[verifier::external_fn_specification] 
pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) 
    -> (r: Result

The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body]. Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body:

/// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. 
/// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does;

#[verifier::external_body] 
pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) 
    ensures 
        // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. 
        r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400,

Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against.

The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. 

Step 5: Reading the spec

The intent artifact is what the team reviews. It’s the plain-language version of the formal spec PDD Kit writes as Verus contracts. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement.

Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. That’s the kind of wiring bug a test suite rarely thinks to look for. The spec also has to talk about SQLite, bcrypt and JWTs without running any of them. It does that with uninterpreted functions, names with no body: customer_on_file(email) and admin_on_file(username) for the rows the database holds, bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) for what bcrypt would say, and token_claims(token, secret) for what a token carries. Verus knows nothing about them except what the trusted contracts from Step 4 promise. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” 

/// The customers row the database holds for 
/// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. 
/// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s 
/// trusted contract says what it is. 
pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq) -> Option; 
... 
/// What bcrypt says about `password` against a 
/// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password 
/// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is 
/// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. 
/// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. 
pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq, hash: Seq) 
    -> Option; 
 
/// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. 
pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq, hash: Seq) -> bool { 
    bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) 
} 

On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code, since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). 

/// The account a login names: the customers row for 
/// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), 
/// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. 
pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option, username: Option) 
    -> Option { 
    match email { 
        Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { 
            Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { 
                id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), 
            None => None, 
        }, 
        None => match username { 
            Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { 
                Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { 
                    id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), 
                None => None, 
            }, 
            None => None, 
        }, 
    } 
} 

Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: 

/// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the 
/// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. 
/// ... 
pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, 
    email: Option, username: Option, password: &str) 
    -> (r: Result) 
    ensures 
        // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. 
        email is None && username is None 
            ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) 
                && m@ == missing_identity_text()), 
        // A token only for the account the login names, with its right 
        // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. 
        r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) 
            && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) 
            && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) 
            && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), 
        // The right password for the named account always gets a 
        // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. 
        (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) 
            && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) 
            ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), 
        // A login naming an account nobody holds gets 
        // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. 
        ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) 
            ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) 
                || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), 
        // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt 
        // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. 
        (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) 
            && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) 
            ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) 
                || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), 
        // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. 
        (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) 
            && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) 
            ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), 
        // The admin role only for an admins row 
        // found by username, with no email sent. 
        (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) 
            && c.role@ == admin_role()) 
            ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) 
                && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), 
        // An email login's token always carries the customer role. 
        (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some) 
            ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) 
                && c.role@ == customer_role()), 
{ 
    unimplemented!() 
} 

The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Its contract ties it to bcrypt_verdict, an uninterpreted model of bcrypt with no axioms:

/// Asks bcrypt whether `password` matches the stored `hash`. 
/// Trusted, not proved: Verus cannot check bcrypt's hashing, 
/// so this wrapper's contract is assumed. 
/// Every password promise of `login_flow` rests on it. 
#[verifier::external_body] 
pub fn check_password(password: &str, hash: &str) -> (r: Result) 
    ensures 
        // bcrypt answers (Ok) exactly when it can read the stored hash. 
        r is Ok <==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) is Some, 
        // Its answer is its verdict: true for the 
        // right password, false for any other. 
        r matches Ok(b) ==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) == Some(b), 
{ 
    bcrypt::verify(password, hash).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) 
} 

The doc comment above it says what rests on it: every password promise of login_flow. Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. 

login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes the value you get when you await it. Nothing promises the future finishes, so a hung query breaks no clause. 

The doc comment on login_flow says so in as many words: 

/// ... No promise the future completes. 
pub async fn login_flow(...) -> (r: Result) 

login_flow stays short because it’s built from smaller proved pieces. lookup_target picks the table. login_core awaits the lookup and calls decide_login, the password gate. issue_token signs the token, or maps a refusal to today’s HTTP error. Each piece has its own contract, and Verus proves login_flow using only those contracts, without re-reading their bodies. Change the body of decide_login and only decide_login gets proved again. 

Here’s the smallest piece, whole, and the start and end of the password gate: 

pub fn lookup_target(email: Option, username: Option) 
    -> (r: Result) 
    ensures 
        // An email, when sent, wins: customers are searched for exactly that email. 
        email matches Some(e) 
            ==> r == Ok::(LookupTarget::CustomerByEmail(e)), 
        // With no email, a username sends the search 
        // to admins for exactly that username. 
        email is None && username matches Some(u) 
            ==> r == Ok::(LookupTarget::AdminByUsername(u)), 
        // With neither, the login is refused for missing an identity. 
        email is None && username is None 
            ==> r == Err::(LoginError::MissingIdentity), 

pub fn decide_login(target: &LookupTarget, found: Option, password: &str) 
    -> (r: Result) 
    ensures 
        // No row found: refused as Unauthorized, 
        // the same answer as a wrong password. 
        found is None 
            ==> r == Err::(LoginError::Unauthorized), 
        // Claims come back only for a found row 
        // whose stored hash matches the password. 
        r is Ok ==> found is Some 
            && password_matches(password@, found->Some_0.password_hash@), 
        // The right password for a found row always gets claims. 
        found matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash@) 
            ==> r is Ok, 
        ... 
        // An admins-table search gives the role text "admin". 
        r matches Ok(c) && target is AdminByUsername ==> c.role@ == admin_role(), 
        // A customers-table search gives the role text "customer". 
        r matches Ok(c) && target is CustomerByEmail ==> c.role@ == customer_role(),

/// Why a login gets no token. 
pub enum LoginError { 
    /// Neither an email nor a username was sent: 400 Bad Request. 
    MissingIdentity, 
    /// No such account, or the password does not match: 401 Unauthorized. 
    Unauthorized, 
    /// bcrypt could not read the stored hash, with its message: 500 Internal. 
    UnreadableHash(String), 
    /// The lookup query failed: 500 Internal, with sqlx's message. 
    Database(sqlx::Error), 
} 

Before the plan comes back to you, two reviewer agents poke holes in the derived formal spec from the intent artifact to ensure a high-quality translation, so that the spec matches what you asked for and doesn’t promise more than a proof could show. The spec refinement runs in the background and takes live user feedback, iterating until reviewers agree that the spec is sound. 

Step 6: Prove, check, close the gaps 

Signing off on the spec is where the developer’s review ends. Everything after it, the implementation and the proof, is checked by machines, which is why this post spends its time on the spec and not the proof. Once the developer signs off, a Build plan stage (Figure 16) hands the approved plan to pdd-prove, which turns it into a small task graph (Figure 16). For login, that’s seven tasks: get login.rs building under Verus inside the backend crate, prove the decision, the token and the whole flow, then write the tests for the trusted wrappers and the end-to-end login. 

Each task runs the same loop: 

  • A coding agent writes the implementation and the proof, and Verus checks them against the derived formal spec. 
  • Anything in the trusted boundary gets the tests the plan called for. 
  • An LLM verifier reads the plan, the specification and the results side by side, and looks for gaps: requirements with no proof and no passing check. Gaps go back to the coding agent until none remain. If the specification itself has a gap, such as two requirements that contradict each other, it comes back to the developer as a decision. 

A proof is only as good as its spec, so pdd-prove checks the spec too. When a model writes its own spec, or is tuned to produce proofs, it tends to land on weak invariants: clauses that verify but rule out almost nothing. They prove something, just rarely the thing you care about. We call that “vibe verification.” That’s why it’s so important to make sure your intent is aligned with the agent and what PDD Kit is great for. 

The loop is strict about not moving the goalposts. If an async construct can’t be expressed in the pinned Verus, the task stops and asks the team instead of switching to a non-async helper or weakening a contract. 

How does PDD Kit remove classes of bugs? The mutation check is how PDD Kit guards against vibe verification. pdd-prove plants one bug per ensures clause in a scratch copy of the code, like refusing everyone or checking the username before the email, and Verus has to reject each mutant on the clause it targets. A mutant that gets through means that clause constrains nothing, and it comes back as a gap. 

Step 7: Review intent alongside verified code

When the tasks pass, pdd-prove opens pull requests. They add a verified/ crate with login_flow, its pieces, their proofs, and the trusted wrappers with their tests, and route the real login handler through login_flow, keeping the existing HTTP status codes. Your verified logic integrates with and hardens your production login path, not a copy of it. 

The developer was able to merge without relying on exhaustive line-by-line review of the generated code. The review had already happened on the intent artifact this whole time, where the team has the final say. We shifted more of the review focus from code review to intent review. The pull request works as a receipt, and its description marks every login requirement as either formally verified or empirically checked. 

Merging is where the proof joins the team’s normal workflow. PDD Kit’s pdd-ship workflow adds the Verus check to CI next to the empirical tests, so every later change to login, by a person or an agent, has to keep proving against the same spec, and a broken proof fails the build like a failing test. And because a proof covers every input, PDD Kit prunes tests that only re-check what’s already proved, such as example-based tests of the password gate, and keeps the ones that guard the trusted boundary, so CI gets stronger and leaner at the same time. 

What the proof does and doesn’t say 

“Fully verified” is easy to oversell, so here’s exactly what we’re claiming.

  • Proved. The bodies of login_flow, login_core, lookup_target, decide_login and issue_token meet their contracts for every input. Login picks the right table, compares the request’s password against the stored hash of the account it names, issues a token with that account’s id and the role its table gives, and refuses everything else with today’s 400, 401 or 500 and no token. 
  • Trusted and tested. The two database lookups, check_password over bcrypt, the clock, token signing, the database error message and the handler’s request unpacking sit outside the proof, each behind an assumed contract the developer accepted. Tests against the real bcrypt, the real SQLite schema and the real router cover them. 
  • Assumed. The Verus, Rust compiler and Z3 (opens in new tab) toolchain, and Verus’s standard library vstd (opens in new tab). 

Why Rust 

PDD Kit only verifies Rust today, since that’s the language Verus works on. If your codebase is already Rust, there’s nothing to migrate. Code in other languages can be ported to Rust and checked against the same spec, and non-Rust projects can call verified Rust through bindings. 

There’s also a less obvious upside. Once reliance on exhaustive line-by-line review has been reduced, readability stops being the main reason to pick a language. You can pick one for speed and safety, and optimize as hard as you want, because any change that breaks the spec fails the proof. 

What to Expect from PDD Kit

PDD Kit is a research prototype, and it only verifies Rust today since that’s the language Verus works on. Code in other languages can be ported to Rust and checked against the same spec, and non-Rust projects can call verified Rust through bindings. Proofs still take real effort, mostly in producing the proof itself, and a clear spec is what keeps that effort down, which is why so much of PDD Kit is about getting intent right first. We’d start where a bug costs the most, such as login, payments, or permissions, and verify the rest of a codebase one piece at a time.

Pet Store’s login is one piece of one app: a spec anyone can read, a Verus proof that the code matches it, and tests for everything the proof takes on trust. We want to be upfront about the weakest links. The guarantees are only as strong as the six trusted pieces, and two carry most of the weight: check_password for every password promise, and the two lookups for every promise about which account a token names. Tests support them, but nothing proves them. We expect that trusted boundary to shrink significantly over time, so a growing share of the code can be formally verified, and we want to find out how far this scales.

What we’re really changing is what people review. Instead of relying mainly on line-by-line review of agent-generated code, a team reviews what it meant, in plain language, and a proof holds the code to it. The plan was always supposed to be the contract, and now the agent actually has to keep it.

Two reviewer agents check the spec, and the pdd-prove workflow plants one bug per clause to catch clauses that verify but rule out nothing. A wrong spec is still possible, which is why PDD Kit emphasizes making requirements explicit, identifying ambiguities, and keeping developers involved in reviewing and approving the spec before verification begins. 

  • The difference is what holds the code to the plan.

    PDD keeps the planning loop from SDD and still uses tests where a proof can’t reach. A test checks some inputs, while a proof establishes that the code satisfies specified properties for all inputs covered by the formal model, under its stated assumptions. 

  • The proof is Rust code annotated with Verus constructs, checked mechanically by Verus using the Z3 solver. It runs wherever your Rust builds: the pdd-prove workflow runs it while proving, and the pdd-ship workflow adds it to your build and CI so a broken proof fails the build. The check is deterministic, with no model involved. Models write the spec, code, and proof, but only a deterministic Verus run decides whether it passed. How long the check takes varies with the size of the code and how hard the proofs are: usually seconds for a small module, up to minutes for a larger codebase.

  • PDD Kit shifts more of the review process toward validating what the code should do, while using formal verification to provide additional assurance that the implementation meets those requirements. Developers review the natural-language plan, the formal spec, and the trusted components that fall outside the scope of the proof. The resulting pull request documents what was formally verified, what was tested, and where additional review may be needed. On the Pet Store full stack web app, this approach reduced reliance on exhaustive line-by-line review of the generated code.

  • We chose Verus because it allows us to verify Rust code directly, aligning with PDD Kit’s focus on integrating formal verification into existing Rust development workflows. Other proof languages (e.g., Lean, F*, Rocq) take different approaches to formal verification, each with its own tradeoffs. The techniques behind PDD Kit could help put them to work as well.
